#8174. Margaret McFarland and the Science of 'Mister Rogers' Neighborhood'

This modest developmental psychologist taught Mister Rogers everything she knew — and then he passed it on to us.

Before Fred Rogers slipped on his shoes and a cardigan, he was a young theology student attending the University of Pittsburgh in the 1950s. There, he studied under developmental psychologist Margaret McFarland, who would end up inspiring, influencing, and actively molding Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood. To say the show would not have been without McFarland is an understatement. Over the course of three decades, Rogers and McFarland met to discuss psychology, upcoming scripts, songs, and of course, children, on a weekly and sometimes daily basis, and her wisdom is imprinted all over the neighborhood.

McFarland was already a large figure in child psychology before ever meeting Fred Rogers. After receiving her doctorate from Columbia and teaching in Melbourne, Australia, McFarland returned to Pittsburgh in 1953 and co-founded the Arsenal Family and Children’s Center with Dr. Benjamin Spock, famous for his studies on child development, and renowned psychologist Erik Erikson, known for coining the eight stages of development and the term “identity crisis.”

Unlike Spock and Erikson, McFarland kept a very low profile throughout her career and wrote very little about her teaching philosophies outside of her dissertation and a single journal article on “development of motherliness.” But her legacy has lived on through her students, Rogers chief among them, and the core tenet of what she taught should sound familiar, even if their origin is not.

When Fred first began his study of child development at Pitt, McFarland help him get in touch with his own childhood memories and feelings. When doing this, she would repeatedly use the phrase, “Anything human is mentionable, and anything mentionable is manageable.” Simply put, it is OK to experience hard feelings openly, and more importantly, when people do this, they find healthier ways to cope. This theme comes up over and over again in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, like when Mister Rogers taught kids about how to get mad without hurting anyone, and feel many other complex feelings. It made for a catchy song and a crucial lesson in emotional intelligence, but like many of Roger’s great ideas, it started with McFarland in the classroom.

In a 2003 interview with the National Endowment for the Humanities, David McCullough boiled down McFarland’s worldview: “What she taught, in essence, is that attitudes aren’t taught, they’re caught. If the attitude of the teacher toward the material is positive, enthusiastic, committed, and excited, the students get that.”

Rogers recalled favorite examples of McFarland putting this into practice in Stuart Omans’ and Maurice O’Sullivan’s book, Shakespeare Plays the Classroom. She had a well-known sculptor from Carnegie Mellon University come to Arsenal but told him not to teach, but to simply be excited about clay in front of the kids.

“And that’s what he did. He came once a week for a whole term, sat with the 4- and 5-year-olds as they played, and he ‘loved’ his clay in front of them,” Rogers said. “The children caught his enthusiasm for it, and that’s what mattered. So, like most good things, ‘teaching’ has to do with honesty.”

McFarland championed a teaching philosophy based on love and compassion. Her friend and colleague Rev. Douglas Nowicki remembers that, “For her, learning could only take place in the context of love. She believed that if a child doesn’t sense that the teacher cares for him or her, then that child will not be able to learn very much.”

Love is perhaps one of the most important supporting characters in Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, more than Mr. McFeely and Daniel Tiger. There were his many ways to say “I love you” and how he always let children watching know he liked them just the way they are, not the things they wear or the way you do their hair. But love may have fallen into the background or been eclipsed by King Friday if it hadn’t been for Margaret.

Pittsburgh play therapist Carole McNamee, one of McFarland’s students, credits her with being one of the sharpest observers. “She could just spot things. She was phenomenal that way,” McNamee shared on the podcast When Fred Met Margaret.

“I’ve never seen anything like it before or since,” Margaret Mary Kimmel, a Ph.D. professor emerita of library and information sciences at Pitt, agreed. Kimmel eventually became a consultant for Mister Rogers and taught a class called Early Childhood and Media, which McFarland helped teach and develop material for. “Margaret talked about how the child interacted with the mother. ‘Did you see her face and the baby’s face? And what about when he started to fuss? How did the mother handle it?’ I learned so much from just watching her watch and describe to the class what was going on between the mother and the baby.”

Fred Rogers may have been the star of the show, but he never wavers from letting children be the center of attention. Even though he cannot see the kids watching at home, his gentle delivery and purposeful pauses helped them feel seen anyway.

This article was originally published on Oct. 24, 2019

#8172. Essentials You Need To Know About Internet Safety For Kids

You kids are growing up with access to everything in the world via the Internet. They'll need restrictions and supervision; here's how to provide it.

Allowing your child to have access to the entire Internet without restriction or supervision would be like setting them loose in the middle of Lagos. Not a good idea, and not a safe bet. And while the Internet can be the perfect place to watch harmless cat videos, research bottomless databases for school reports, and play games that educate and entertain them, it’s also a place where phishing, social network harassment, and scams abound. That’s why it’s up to you to educate your children about what’s safe and what’s not — and to know what to keep an eye on for yourself.

According to Wired Safety — a leading online safety, education, and help organization — cyberbullying begins to expand by age eight. And from there it reaches far and wide, with 43 percent of teens aged 13 to 17 reporting that they have experienced some sort of cyberbullying in the past year. Help your child learn how to deal with cyberbullies (and how to not become one) by having them “graduate” from the Carnegie Cyber Academy — an interactive educational tool developed by Carnegie Mellon University to teach proper Web etiquette and how to defend yourself from “Cyber Villains.”

No matter what age your child is, setting boundaries with the Internet is imperative. The types of websites your kids visit, the search engines they use, and the content they have access to should all play into the restrictions and limitations you set on your devices and through your Internet provider. Enough Is Enough compiled a list of kid-safe search engines that are more reliable than a Google Safe Search. Additionally, most cable and Internet providers, such as XFinity and Comcast allow you to block websites by URL, keyword, and device accessing them. If that’s not enough, there are services such as The Children’s Internet that offer children safe, age-appropriate Internet experience available for a monthly fee. If you do allow your child to use a mobile device, then use a kid-friendly mobile device.

A good lesson to instill in children is to be as cautious and careful on the Internet as they are in real life. Challenge them to ask themselves, “Would I tell this or act like this to a stranger in person?” and, “Would I be comfortable with this if a responsible adult were looking over my shoulder?” This allows children to acknowledge that everyone is a person behind the computer screen.

Just because you have restrictions or blocks on devices doesn’t mean that you don’t have to keep an eye on your children’s activity online. Enough Is Enough encourages families to keep all devices in shared or open space in the home — such as the living room. Make sure you know who your child is communicating with online, as well as their online history.

#8170. The Best Back-to-School Books For Every Age and Stage

The time when kids go back to school is full of hope and excitement. It can also be a time of nervousness and apprehension. And, for as long as most people can remember, one of the greatest ways to cure the blues, for kids and adults, is to read a good book.

Not all great back-to-school books have to be specifically about school or jitters. But sometimes that kind of thing helps. From Pre-K kiddos to high schoolers, here’s a selection of great books that will help kids feel calmer, brighter, and more confident about heading back to the classroom.

You might remember Amelia Bedelia as a bumbling housekeeper, but her more recent adventures as a younger woman are great for young ones. This picture book contains some of the same wordplay of the old books, with a great message.

This board book is part of Usborne’s “Very First Questions and Answers” series and, as such, addresses the basic question of why school, or some form of education and structure, is important. Neither pandering nor confusing, this book is literally designed to explain the concept to very young school-age ones. The talking points here take some of the guesswork out of a parent’s speech, so you may want to read it quickly to yourself before sharing with your kid.

This sweet picture book isn’t about school specifically at all. But it is a book about how kids can plan for and manage their disappointments. The titular mouse, Clementine, worries about all sorts of things going wrong. But, the key lesson here is to plan for “Uh Ohs.” Great for parents who have anxious kids or children who feel like everything has to be perfect.

Ages: Pre-K, Kindergarten, and 1st Grade.

As first chapter books go, Abby Hanlon’s brilliant Dory Fantasmagory books are really without any peers. Hilarious, heartfelt, and easily readable for kids just starting chapter books, the Dory books don’t just make kids feel better about being kids; the books actually capture the hilarious nature of little kid logic.

All of Dory’s adventures are good for back-to-school jitters, but the second book, The Real True Friend, is perhaps the best primer for meeting new kids and trying to fit in.

Judy Blume’s immortal book is technically the third in a series that began with Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing. Focused on the trials and tribulations of 5th and 6th graders, and their changing feelings toward the world, this book has only gotten better since 1980. The humor and realism still work, over 40 years later, and the analog nature of this very recent past can be nothing but positive for modern kids.

Ages: Late Elementary school and Middle School

That’s right, the classic Choose Your Own Adventure books are back. And now, with new, slick covers for the 2020s. Why are these good for back-to-school? As nuts as some of the classic Choose Your Own Adventure books are, the thing that makes these stories so great for emerging readers is the fact that it’s totally okay to fail.

The bite-sized adventures are also great for kids who think that they don’t enjoy reading. These books are modern classics for the specific reason that kids feel like they’re in control.

Imagine a series sort of like Harry Potter, but instead of humans, you’re following a bunch of talking dragons. That might not fully represent Wings of Fire, but it does give you a sense of the appeal of this series. With different dragon characters that every kid can identify with, Wings of Fire is a truly inclusive series, which is impressive since most of the characters are fire-breathing reptiles.

Sometimes the best way to educate kids about the classics is to barely disguise the classics at all. The brilliant thing about George O’Connor’s Olympians graphic novel books is that these are fairly straightforward takes on classic Greek mythology. Middle-grade kids will love the awesome illustrations, but they’ll also be way ahead in history class.

The story of siblings finding a secret world within a normal city has become an instant classic since 2012. Not exactly coded for back-to-school, middle-grade or early middle-school kids should read the Wildwood series for one reason: Other bookworm kids will have probably read these books, too.

Ages: 5th grade, 6th grade, or Middle-School

A graphic novel from author and illustrator Jerry Craft, New Kid is perhaps the perfect contemporary back-to-school book for older kids. Focused on a 7th grader named Jordan Banks, the book is all about feeling like an outsider, relative to both class and race. A good point of view for all kinds of kids.

If your kid likes this one, there are others in the series, including Class Act and School Trip.

Sunrise on the Reaping (Hunger Games series)

Yes, after all these years, Suzanne Collins' Hunger Games universe is still relevant and great for older kids. The newest 2025 book, Sunrise on the Reaping, is the second in the Hunger Games prequels series that began with The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes in 2020. In some ways, these prequels are better than the classic Hunger Games books. But if your kiddos get hooked, the other books are waiting for them after they finish the new ones.

The Complete Collected Poems of Maya Angelou

Sometimes tweens and teens need a little bit of inspiration. And that comfort and inspiration don’t always have to come in the form of narratives. Instead, why not turn to the poetry of one of the greats? Every kid who has ever had a deep feeling about something will relate to at least one of Maya Angelou’s poems. And, in terms of centering oneself before the stress of back-to-school, nobody touches the soul quite like Angelou.

#8169. Why Do I Get Dizzy When I Stand Up? Experts Say No, This Isn't Normal

“If something is repeatedly interfering with how you feel or function, you deserve a thoughtful evaluation.”

It happens when you get up from your desk at work, from playing on the floor with your kids, even when you get out of bed first thing in the morning. Lately, whenever you go from lying or sitting to standing, you get a little dizzy. You have to pause and close your eyes, maybe grab onto something solid, and wait a few seconds before taking off. So what gives? Why do you get dizzy when you stand up now, and is it normal?

Well, medical experts agree that getting dizzy every time you stand up is categorically not normal, and it’s worth making an appointment with your doctor to investigate why it happens to you. They say the answer is likely something easy to fix, and anything impacting your daily functioning is worth the investigation.

Adjusting your blood flow to your current activity level is one of those things our brain does all on its own that we don’t really appreciate fully until it goes wrong.

“When someone stands up, gravity pulls blood toward the lower half of the body, and the nervous system has to respond quickly to maintain blood flow to the brain. If that adjustment doesn’t happen efficiently, you can feel lightheaded, see spots, or feel as though you’re about to faint,” says Dr. Motisola Lewis, MD, internal medicine physician and founder of Lewis Medical NY.

For women in their 30s, 40s, and 50s, dizziness upon standing can be a symptom of many different things.

“Some of the most common causes are dehydration, not eating or drinking enough, low blood pressure, anemia, blood loss, and medication side effects. In women in their 30s through 50s, I also think about heavy menstrual bleeding, hormonal transitions, and medications that can affect blood pressure or heart rate. Sometimes there is more than one contributing factor,” Lewis explains.

It’s also important to distinguish between dizziness and vertigo so you can accurately describe your experience to your doctor.

“If they feel lightheaded, faint, or like they might pass out, I would think about blood pressure issues, especially orthostatic hypotension. Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in blood pressure with standing. Dehydration, medication side effects or interactions, blood sugar fluctuations, cardiovascular issues, and other medical conditions can also cause lightheadedness,” says Dr. Kim Bell, a doctor of physical therapy who specializes in dizziness, vertigo, balance problems, and fall prevention.

“If they describe more of a brief spinning sensation when they get up, I would also want to rule out benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or BPPV, which is the most common inner ear cause of vertigo. BPPV can cause momentary dizziness or spinning with position changes such as sitting up in bed or getting out of bed.”

If you’ve made an appointment with your doctor to discuss your dizziness, ask yourself a few questions and log the answers for a week or two before you go. Pay attention to what the dizziness feels like, what movement or position triggers it, and how long it lasts, Bell says. “Those details can provide important clues about the cause.”

If it happens once, OK, maybe you were just dehydrated. But if it happens frequently, no, that’s not normal at all, Lewis and Bell agree.

“I would not want someone to assume that their height, age, stress level, or tendency to ‘stand up too fast’ explains recurring dizziness without actually investigating the cause,” says Bell.

If you’ve ever had a doctor chalk up your dizziness to standing up too fast, anxiety, or literally just being too tall (this really happens), look for a second opinion.

“Women deserve to be heard before their symptoms are explained away. Many women are exceptionally good at pushing through discomfort. They get the children ready, go to work, care for their families, and carry on even when they don’t feel well. Sometimes they normalize their symptoms because they’ve been told that what they’re experiencing is just stress, aging, or something they have to live with. But if you're consistently dizzy when you stand, exhausted despite sleeping, experiencing a racing heart, or struggling to function the way you used to, it’s worth asking why,” says Lewis.

This doesn’t mean your dizziness is pointing to a rare or serious condition; usually the cause is something simple and totally treatable, Lewis adds.

If you’re experiencing certain symptoms along with dizziness, it warrants a more urgent assessment, Lewis says. Here are the symptoms that Bell and Lewis say would make them want to see you ASAP:

If you experience new neurological symptoms, including sudden weakness or numbness on one side, confusion, double vision, difficulty speaking, or a sudden severe headache, that’s your sign to head to your nearest emergency room, Lewis notes.

If you’ve heard about POTS lately, well, that’s because it’s becoming a lot more common.

All around the world, studies show health experts are diagnosing more people than ever before with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS: an autonomic nervous system disorder that causes your heart to beat faster than normal when you go from sitting or lying down to standing up. Unsurprisingly, dizziness upon standing is one of its hallmark symptoms. The condition can be caused by severe viral infections; public health experts believe the COVID-19 pandemic caused a massive number of previously healthy people to develop POTS.

While it might be in the zeitgeist right now, Lewis says POTS is not the most common explanation for dizziness upon standing. Women in their 30s, 40s, and 50s can have so much happening in their bodies that the dizziness may be the result of more than one factor as well — think sleep disruptions, hormonal changes, and iron deficiency.

If anything in your life, like getting dizzy when you stand, is interfering with how you feel or function, “you deserve a thoughtful evaluation” from your healthcare provider, Lewis says.

If you only do one job in your garden this weekend, raise patio planters on pot risers so roots don’t sit in wet soil and rot in this wetter weather. Sliding risers underneath pots only takes a few minutes yet it drastically improves drainage to stop soil from sitting soggy. And it's waterlogged soil – not the cold weather – that's the number one reason potted plants die over winter. So, this quick container gardening trick to keep soil well-drained will have a huge impact on your plants' health, and whether or not they survive into spring.

You see, roots need to breathe: just like we humans, they take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide. In saturated soil, water displaces air and roots suffocate. Some plants can cope longer than others but the wet, oxygen-depleted soil also creates the perfect environment for fungus and bacteria to thrive, leading to rotting roots. The more roots are compromised, the less able a plant is able to fight the attack, and a vicious cycle begins. And this is such a common problem in fall, making this task one of the most vital October gardening jobs.

Take a closer look at your patio planters and you'll find there's very little room for water to escape from the drainage hole of a pot sitting directly on paving or decking, even if it's not set in a saucer. Now that’s fine in summer with low rainfall and high evaporation rates, but once fall clouds roll in, higher rainfall quickly causes water to permanently pool in pot bases.

What’s more, when winter arrives and that water freezes and expands, ice can rupture root cells, causing severe and often fatal damage. So, even when plants are plenty hardy enough to cope with the chill of winter, they kick the bucket because they simply can’t survive with their roots in permanently saturated soil.

The good news is that there's a super-simple solution to this widespread problem, and it's one of the most fundamental of container gardening ideas you can DIY on a budget. First of all, get rid of any plant saucers as they hold water around the roots. Then raise your pots up off the ground – just an inch is plenty – to free that all-important drainage hole and allow rainfall to pass right through the soil. You can buy pot toes, pot risers or plant stands, and there are options for every budget and garden style, or simply use whatever you've already got such as flat pebbles or old bricks.

All plants will benefit from their pots being raised through fall and winter, but especially plants that need great drainage like lavender and santolina.

Raising pots in fall will also protect your paving or deck from becoming marked with pot rings or algae, saving you the time and expense of scrubbing these off in spring. An essential step in winterizing your garden, raising pots will also help to protect containers from cracking, particularly terracotta. Part of the Weekend Win series, raising pots to keep roots safe from rot is one of those easy jobs that brings a big reward.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Let’s start with the simplest, cheapest option for this essential part of fall gardening. Pot toes, also called pot feet, sit under the base of a planter with a raised section jutting out to hold it steady against the container’s outer wall. You need at least three toes for each pot, and more for larger planters. As well as being practical, some pot toes can add a decorative touch.

Plastic triangle pot toes typically come in bulk packs, and look for designs like this that can be vertically stacked to create sharper drainage if required. They’re cheap and effective, and work well on uneven decking and paving.

For bigger pots, you need more robust pot toes, and although they're more expensive, they're also more durable. Do check the size as some are uselessly small – these measure 3.1” x 1.6” so will support planters up to 20” in diameter.

Decorative pot toes, typically made of resin, may be adorable but are only suitable for very small pots as the surface area the planter will sit on is often tiny. Keep these for that little pot of pansies on your patio table.

Pot risers differ from pot toes because they’re designed to sit under the planter, often out of sight. Because most offer more surface area for pot bases to sit on, they’re a good bet for bigger, heavier planters or more fragile materials like terracotta. You’ll also find them a stable option for bowl planters and pots with sides that slope sharply outwards.

These solid rubber pot risers are textured for grip so stay in place. They’re a practical solution for bigger planters of all shapes as you can use as many as you need, and with 24 in a pack, they’re great value.

This purpose-made plastic plant stand carries up to 500lbs so supports the weight of bigger containers well. Suitable for pots with a base of up to 16” diameter, it can easily be cut to size to sit under smaller planters.

Bulk packs of plastic plant-riser discs are a cheap solution but check they’re made of durable material designed for outdoors, and only use for small pots. Many pot inserts are sold as plant risers and aren’t strong enough for this job.

Of course, another option to keep that all-important drainage hole free is to pop pots on a plant stand. This adds style to your patio and it's quick and easy if you want to rearrange pots. Be sure to look for rust-resistant powder-coated metal which won’t create lasting stains on your paving or decking.

Equipping your patio pots with plant stands needn’t be expensive as this 5-pack of metal designs proves. Heights range from 3.4" to 7.28" and diameters from 7.97" to 11.42' to accommodate plenty of pots.

If aesthetics are high on your garden list, Target has a great range of architectural plant stands from Achla Designs such as this contemporary beauty. It’s made from wrought iron with a powder-coated finish and striking good looks.

A single plant stand that can accommodate all your smaller pots is often a cheaper option than buying lots of individual risers, and this handy corner design is also available in white, with each shelf supporting 50lbs.

#8166. How To Make Summer Memories That Stick

Summer’s behind us. What memories did you make?

Labor day is upon us and as I celebrate the ending of the chaotic mess that is summer for parents, I also can’t help but feel a little wistful. Did I make the most of the summer? Or, more to the point, have I made lasting memories for my kids?

The answer to that, I think, is yes. But the memories are not found in volumes of ice cream, the rides at the county fair, the hours of pool time and picnics, or the (shockingly expensive) songs and bonding they had at camps. I believe that in the long term these simple joys will become part of a happy and balanced childhood, but they’re not the kind of thing they look back on and say, “remember when …?”

The “remember when” moments are a different kind of fun — Type 2 fun.

As former Fatherly editor Julia Holmes explained in her wonderful essay on memory and adventures, there are varying levels of fun. “The ‘fun scale,’” she writes, “which first circulated in climbing books and media in the 1980s, divides outdoor recreation into three major categories. At one end of the scale is Type 1: You expect to enjoy yourself and you do (a day at the beach). At the other end of the scale is Type 3: not even remotely fun, catastrophically bad, something never to be repeated (shipwrecked). Somewhere between those extremes is the perfect fun, the kind of fun that pushes you past yourself and (hopefully) delivers you back to yourself in better condition — stronger, happier, full of fresh gratitude for comfort and company.”

Type 2 fun is the stuff of memories. When we tell a great story about travel or adventure — one that’s worth retelling throughout life — there is usually an edge to it. There are barriers overcome, there is a sketchy or frightening moment, there are lessons learned.

I think about Type 2 fun all the time. As a distance runner and cyclist and outdoors person who remembers the first time they got hypothermia fondly (it’s a good story!), I embrace such “fun” and try to bring my kids into it. As a dad, I know that summers, with the kids out of school and the weather cooperating is a great time to go after it.

So, as we stare down Labor Day, I wonder to myself, how’d I do?

This summer, if you are to look at my 8-year-old’s skinned knees, I think some memories were made. We daily took to the trails and roads and pump track to bike. There were falls, tears, and an awesome amount of getting back on the bike with a chin held high. One of his favorite stories to tell was actually from last summer when we were mountain biking together, attached, tandem-style. It was hot, buggy, and we had already had a minor crash (or two) along the rocky trail. At one point, there was a ledge that required you to walk your bike, single file, over a small cliff. I asked my son to go to the other side and wait, the better for him to watch as I awkwardly pushed the long tandem bike along the thin ledge, lost my balance and, rather than fall 20 feet to the forest floor, tossed the bike and leaned into the rock. I steadied myself as the bike crashed below. Thirty minutes later, we had were back up top and on the trail again — with a story to tell.

For my older child, I might have gone a little hard on the Type 2 fun this summer. I offered to pick up my teen and their best friend from overnight camp and take them on their first real backpacking trip this year. I marked the maps, packed the food, and neatly stored our tents, stoves, water purifiers, headlamps, and sleeping bags for a three-night, four day trip on The Long Trail in Vermont. The more serious ascent was to happen on day 1, leaving the rest of the trip for a rolling hike, out and back, to give them a pleasant taste for one of my favorite pastimes.

The Gods of Type 2 fun had other plans. First of all, the parking lot on the map simply wasn’t where it should have been, so we wound our way through country roads to the next lot, miles away and downhill from the planned start. In the new parking lot, a sign informed us that a shelter had moved a few miles further. The short of it: A good hike became a formidable trek. Three days, 18.34 miles, and 4,698 feet (up!) later, the kids refused to camp a third night in the woods, demanding to hike straight to the car and go get a hotel. We did just that. I stopped for milkshakes on the way, but somehow, years from now, I don’t think the truck stop shakes are what they’re going to remember about their time on The Long Trail.

This weekend, I think I’m going to take the family to Coney Island. The kids will grab hot dogs, we’ll all ride on the Wonder Wheel, walk down the beach and share the breeze. We’ve made enough memories this summer — and everyone needs a little forgettable fun too.

#8164. How To Get Fantastic Sleep

Are parents doomed to a lifetime of chasing after good sleep?

On a tip from a savvy movie critic, I took my 7-year-old out to see his second ever Marvel movie the other day (he's a big fan of Norse mythology so he's seen Thor: Ragnarok and sorta liked it). We sat back, donning our 3D glasses (he was very into the novelty of this) and took in The Fantastic Four: First Steps. What a pleasant surprise. The movie is, in fact, as my movie critic colleague promised, The Best Marvel Movie for Families.

For the kids, there’s a lot to love. There are the action montages, a bright retro futuristic setting, a visual style that is gee-whiz superhero cool, but in a comic way — shiny and light and not over the top. The movie is just more palatable for kids than most other Marvel movies, emotionally and cognitively. The superheroes are relatable as family but they also play the part of role models well, interacting with and caring deeply about the public they serve. The villain, too, is not so much motivated by evil but by an unstoppable appetite (for planets, granted) that he is actively trying to rid himself of. A little sympathy goes a long way to take the teeth out of a monster. But most importantly there’s Franklin, the baby.

The Fantastic Four are a family and have arguments and issues that are familiar to all kids. One big one is the strain (and joys) that having a baby puts on, well, everyone. I especially loved seeing Reed Richards and Sue Storm, superheroes with doctorates who no doubt have seen their share of sleep debt, complain about tiredness. Even genius superheroes can’t face the superheroic task that is getting baby to bed. It’s a tension that gets the screen time it deserves. Just ask any parent.

Sleep has been on my mind a lot lately. I always thought that I would crush sleep once my baby grew up, but some 6 years later I realize maybe it wasn’t the baby? I’ve never met someone who doesn’t have a tenuous relationship with sleep. When I was in physical prime either during my senior high school years as a soccer player and middle distant runner or during my marathon-happy thirties, I slept so very soundly. At least that’s how I remember it.

Now that I’m older I juggle more — so much more — work out a little less and do a lot more staring at the ceiling in the middle of the night. With age, I maybe need to admit, I need an assist.

I’ve only just started to give sleep tracking a fair shake. I’ve been pairing up a new Samsung Galaxy 8 watch with a Samsung Galaxy Ring (I’ve been a Samsung man since I converted to their Flip phone, which pairs seamlessly together, requiring no third-party apps).

So what have I found? That data is in fact motivating. I won’t get too into the weeds but I will tell you that late night snacks, screens, night caps, and work are bad for my sleep. Evening walks, reading, and days with lighter fare and more quality workouts lead to more quality sleep.

It’s all fairly obvious stuff, but what the tracking does is force the attention. Good sleep matters and is, for those of us without babies, a fairly controllable thing. We can create habits that help sleep. We can choose to prioritize our health and well being. Stats don’t tell us what to do, but they do show what our current priorities.

When my son was a sleepless baby (he really was the worst) the only two priorities I had were to keep him healthy (alive) and to find sleep. My world is a little easier now and my list of priorities has grown immensely. I want to be outdoors more, to find new fitness, to take on new passions (birding is kind of fun, everyone), to embrace a new phase of marriage, to learn new skills, and meet my kids where they are. But sometimes you have to remember the basics. Without good sleep, everything is more difficult. Only a superhero can defeat the eater of worlds on a new parent’s sleep schedule. The rest of us need all the help we can get.

#8163. 10 Make-Ahead Thanksgiving Sides That Genuinely Reheat Well

Assemble them ahead of time and Turkey Day will be a breeze.

Maybe you’re trying to avoid a spicy mother-in-law and want to be sequestered in the kitchen all day on Thanksgiving (and more power to you). But for most people, the idea of having your house full of family and friends and being trapped standing at the stove the whole time isn’t ideal. That’s where these make-ahead sides that actually reheat well come into play. You see, no one wants clumped-up, days-old, dried-out mashed potatoes on Turkey Day, nor do they want to be hand-mashing while everyone laughs and drinks in the living room. But with recipes like these, a happy medium is possible.

Sweet potato casserole is a must at every Thanksgiving feast. When else is it socially acceptable to serve a vegetable topped with marshmallows? All The Healthy Things’ recipe includes special notes of orange and brown butter, as well as a few notes about different ways to prep the recipe ahead of time and save yourself some work the day-of.

Just go ahead and whip up All The Healthy Things’ slow cooker mashed potatoes in advance; they’ll microwave beautifully, or fit right back into the slow cooker on “keep warm.” This way you can focus all your efforts on the turkey gravy.

Make Simply LaKita’s corn pudding ahead of time so you can use that oven space for other things on Thanksgiving. Her reheating instructions say you can put the whole dish back into the oven at 300 degrees, or just put individual portions in the microwave.

Who knew you could make stuffing ahead of time? Just follow Damn Delicious’ recipe up to step five (which is when you combine all the ingredients in the baking dish). Instead of putting it straight into the oven, let it cool and pop it in the fridge overnight, then bake when you’re ready to serve the following day.

Just like the stuffing, you can make this green bean casserole from Damn Delicious nearly to completion — just hold off on popping the breadcrumbs and fried shallots on top until you’re ready to bake it. Then, they’ll come out crispy and perfect and right on time.

Princess Pinky Girl’s scalloped potato recipe is perfect for planning ahead. You can bake it completely and reheat individual portions, assemble but wait to bake, or even bake it halfway and finish it off on the day of Thanksgiving dinner.

Damn Delicious’ make-ahead yeast rolls are perfectly plump and fluffy, ideal for spreading with butter or mopping up gravy (mmm). Her post explains that you can refrigerate the rolls overnight so they double in size before baking, or simply bake, freeze, and reheat, so you can make them much farther in advance.

Fried apples may not be a staple on every Thanksgiving table, but in the South, they often make an appearance at holiday meals. Simply LaKita’s recipe is simple and easy, and includes instructions for reheating the apples in the microwave or a skillet.

This mac and cheese recipe from Averie Cooks is incredibly easy and will definitely reheat beautifully. It’s so creamy and saucy, it won’t dry out like a premade baked mac tends to.

Whether you choose to reheat them in the microwave or the oven, Simply LaKita promises her candied yams come out tender and flavorful every time. You can make them up to two days in advance, so this could be one of your Tuesday evening preps.

Which of these recipes will you try this year? Personally, I’m eyeing that green bean casserole pretty hard...

Want more beautiful coneflowers next year? A few simple October tasks can help your perennials do exactly that...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Coneflowers are one of my favorite flowers to grow for their cheerful summer blooms and their ability to attract pollinators. I love that they tend to just get on with everything, with or without my help. That being said, though...

Well, even when their petals have faded and the garden is beginning to wind down for winter, though, I wouldn't advise you to forget about your coneflowers just yet. In fact, October is a useful time to give these perennials a little attention, helping them prepare for the colder months while making the most of what they still have to offer.

The good news is that coneflowers (Echinacea spp.) don't need a complicated fall care routine. With that in mind, then, what do these pretty blooms want from us all when the weather starts to turn?

I feel it's my duty to point out that one of the most helpful things you can do for coneflowers resist the temptation to cut everything back, as their dried flower heads can provide food for hungry birds, while leaving healthy stems standing can add structure to the garden through winter.

There are, however, a few things worth checking before the weather turns colder. From deciding which seedheads to leave in place to spotting diseased foliage, here are three October tasks I'd prioritize for healthier coneflowers and a more wildlife-friendly garden.

If there's one thing I'd encourage gardeners to do with their coneflowers in October, it's to leave the healthy seedheads standing. Once the colorful petals have dropped, the central cones dry out and contain seeds that birds can forage on through fall and winter.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

American goldfinches are particularly fond of coneflower seeds, and watching these bright-yellow birds perch on the sturdy stems and pick out the seeds is a lovely reminder that a garden can keep giving long after its flowers have faded. Other seed-eating birds (including your very own birth month bird) may also visit, depending on your region and the species growing in your garden.

I'd resist the urge to deadhead every faded flower simply to make the border look tidy. Instead, leave plenty of healthy seedheads in place and let them provide a natural food source. They'll also add interesting shapes and texture to the winter garden, particularly when dusted with frost.

One thing to keep in mind is that not every coneflower cultivar produces the same amount of viable seed. Some highly bred double-flowered varieties may offer less to birds than simpler, single-flowered forms. If supporting wildlife is a priority, consider growing native purple coneflower (Echinacea purpurea) and other varieties known to produce seed.

Although I'd leave healthy coneflower stems standing, I wouldn't ignore signs of disease. October is a good time to look over the foliage and remove material that's badly affected by fungal problems, particularly powdery mildew.

Powdery mildew often appears as a pale, powdery coating on leaves and stems. It can be more noticeable late in the growing season, especially when plants have experienced humid conditions or poor air circulation. A little cosmetic damage isn't necessarily a reason to remove an otherwise healthy plant, but heavily affected foliage shouldn't simply be left to sit in the garden.

I'd stick to the Three D's rule and cut out badly diseased material using clean pruning tools and dispose of it appropriately rather than adding it to a home compost pile. This helps reduce the amount of infected debris left around the plant.

It's important to be selective here. I wouldn't cut every coneflower down just because some leaves are looking tired. Healthy stems and seedheads can remain standing for birds and winter interest, while diseased material can be removed as needed.

My final October task would be to prepare coneflowers for winter without disturbing them unnecessarily. In most gardens, established coneflowers are hardy perennials that don't require extensive protection, but a little attention to the soil can help.

I'd check that the soil around the plants isn't compacted and make sure water can drain away rather than pooling around the crowns. Coneflowers generally prefer well-drained soil, and persistently wet conditions can cause problems during colder weather. If the ground is dry, I may water the plants before the soil freezes, particularly if conditions have been unusually dry. And a light layer of mulch can help moderate soil temperatures and protect roots, although I'd avoid piling it directly over the crown.

Most importantly, I'd leave the main cleanup until spring. Once the weather warms and new growth begins to emerge, I can cut back the old stems before they get in the way. Waiting also means I don't remove useful seedheads too early or disturb wildlife that may be using the garden through winter.

Basically, coneflowers don't need much fuss in October, and that's part of their appeal. By leaving healthy seedheads for goldfinches, removing diseased foliage when necessary, and protecting the root zone without cutting everything down, I can help these reliable perennials get through winter while keeping the garden useful to wildlife.

Rather than treating fall as a time to strip the garden bare, I'd see it as an opportunity to be more selective. A few standing stems can provide food, shelter, and winter interest – and when spring arrives, the coneflowers will be ready to grow again. And you can't say better than that, right?

#8158. 20 Buddy Shows To Watch After You Finish 'Friends' For The Umpteenth Time

Time to cue up your next comfort-watch obsession.

You will never, and I mean never, catch me shaming anyone over how many times they’ve binge-watched Friends. If anyone can recite Ross's meltdown from "The One Where No One's Ready" from heart, it's yours truly. If you handed me a pencil and sketch pad right now, I could probably draw a pretty decent rendering of Monica's apartment from memory. Friends, for so many of us, is like the TV equivalent of your softest sweatshirt; it's just something that makes you instantly feel better, something you want to slide into at the end of a long day. Alas, even the coziest rewatch eventually runs out of episodes, leaving you staring at the screen like Joey staring at a menu devoid of meatball subs.

The good news is that the things you actually love about Friends aren’t exclusive to our favorite funny New Yorkers (and that signature orange Central Perk couch). There are lots of truly incredible shows out there that’ve also nailed the buddy-comedy magic. So whether you're on the hunt for a replacement friend group or craving another workplace crew that feels like family, here’s what you can queue up next.

If You’re Looking for Another Friend Group to Adopt

I don’t want to ruffle any feathers here, but Living Single actually came out a full year before Friends… and yet it doesn’t get nearly as much love as it deserves. Watch it and try to deny the overlap: a core group of twentysomethings, a New York brownstone, romantic chaos to spare. Queen Latifah has even publicly hinted that NBC borrowed the concept; I'm just saying. Either way, Khadijah, Synclaire, Régine, and Max are an all-time friend group, and Kyle and Max’s bickering is will-they-won’t-they at its finest.

Obviously, right? Just swap the coffee shop for a dive bar and you’ve got New Girl. Jess, Nick, Schmidt, Winston, and Cece are so funny you’ll literally be crying from laughing (the best kind of tears). Plus, we can probably all agree that Nick and Jess give Ross and Rachel a serious run for their money. Bonus: True American is the Friends’ Thanksgiving football game for a new generation.

Happy Endings only got three seasons before ABC pulled the plug, so be aware of that going in. It’s expiration dating, if you will. And while that remains a crime, it just means you can binge the whole thing in one weekend... which you should, because Damon Wayans Jr.’s Brad and Eliza Coupe’s Jane are one of TV’s best married couples, full stop.

For many fans, this is likely the most direct descendant of Friends on the list: five pals, one bar booth, and a nine-season mystery to see who one of the group ends up with. People have many opinions about that finale, but you can’t argue that the journey to get there is pure comfort food.

Joan, Toni, Maya, and Lynn may have been a dysfunctional group of friends, but they loved each other fiercely and honestly through all the ups and downs. To this day, they remain the L.A. girl gang I wish I could have been a part of in my 20s (fine, I still do — Tracee Ellis Ross, let’s be best friends please). The series recently left Netflix, but you can stream all eight seasons on Pluto TV for free. Maybe if we all stream enough, they’ll give us some sort of reunion!

Derry Girls is kind of like an Irish coming-of-age version of our Central Perk crew. Hear me out. Erin, Orla, Clare, Michelle, and James (the "wee English fella") are a group of teens navigating Catholic school and family histrionics in '90s Northern Ireland. It's hilarious, but also surprisingly heartfelt. Plus, episodes are short enough to make it an easy rewatch.

As a workin’ mom myself, I can think of few shows more relatable than this raunchy and delightfully real series. Meet Kate, Anne, Frankie, and Jenny: a group of moms who took a mommy-and-me class together and then became part of each other's mom circle. They experience all the stuff that moms need someone to talk to about, from pumping mishaps at work to postpartum spirals and terrible bosses. And, yes, relationship snags and some truly questionable decision-making along the way. All seven seasons are ready, so you can binge straight through a long weekend if you're feeling froggy.

Camille, Tye, Quinn, and Angie are four college besties now navigating their 30s... in heels, uptown, with an extra spicy group chat. They show up for each other through the big friendship milestones, like meltdowns and messy exes, and whew, they do it all in style (prepare for serious wardrobe envy). Created by Girls Trip writer Tracy Oliver, it’s edgy and smart, not to mention wildly bingeable.

If one of the things you love most about Friends is the dynamic between Joey and Chandler, you cannot go another minute without tuning into Scrubs for J.D. and Turk. The bromance is beyond real (Zach Braff and Donald Faison are BFFs outside of the show, too). The fantasy sequences are undeniably some of the best to ever exist. And somehow this deeply funny show can turn on a dime and have you ugly-crying at any minute. Even better: The revival is back on ABC for another season, so this one’ll keep you busy for a while.

Abbi and Ilana’s friendship is a little bit of everything: supportive, chaotic, always a little too high. They’re two twentysomething women trying to make it in New York City and all that entails, between dating disasters and struggling to make rent. It’s raunchy, it’s feminist, it’s unapologetically millennial, it’s 100% worth your time.

Available to stream on Hulu and Paramount+

Yep, a show about a ride-or-die duo that is named Ride or Die. Prepare for a little disappointment right up front because, despite it being a No. 1 show for the streamer, Prime Video canceled this absolute gem after just one season. There’s still hope it’ll get picked up somewhere else, though, so go watch how brilliant Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer are as best friends on the lam… and then spam Prime Video with positive reviews.

When their husbands leave them for each other, Grace and Frankie are not exactly simpatico. You couldn’t find two more different women if you tried. But grief and growth and time have a funny way of making people see what’s right in front of them, and in this case, that leads to Grace and Frankie becoming best friends. Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin are perfection as this uptight/hippie odd couple.

Make no mistake: The central love story in Insecure is the friendship between Issa and Molly, and one of the best parts is how refreshingly honest and authentic the series portrays it. These are best friends who love each other, hurt each other, find their way back, rinse and repeat. It’s funny and it’s messy and it’s just so real.

Who would have thought that Selena Gomez, Steve Martin, and Martin Short would give us one of the best TV trios of our time? Yet here they are, three memorable characters who bond over true-crime podcasts and, well, actual murders in their building. Their cross-generational friendship feels totally natural thanks to their killer chemistry, which we’ll get even more of when Season 6 heads to London starting Dec. 8.

I would watch anything with Christina Applegate. I would watch anything with Linda Cardellini (speaking of, go watch her in Crystal Lake right now if you like horror). So, it just makes sense that I would be utterly obsessed with this series about two women who meet in a grief group and develop a ridiculously tight, beautiful, complicated friendship. It’s darker than anything you’ll see at Central Perk, but it’s got just as much heart.

Fair warning: This show will make you feel sick over the fact that you can’t have Shawn and Gus as friends in real life. Still, it’s worth watching Shawn fake psychic powers to solve crimes while Gus reluctantly (always reluctantly) tags along. Their rapid-fire riffs are unrivaled, and you’ll get tinges of Joey and Chandler’s rapport when you hear their ridiculous nicknames for each other. Eight seasons plus three movies means plenty to binge. Just don’t forget to look for the pineapple hidden in every episode!

Available to stream on Peacock and Prime Video

If You Want Work Friends Who Feel Like Family

Monica stans, rise up! Here, we get the local government version of our favorite Type A personality in Leslie Knope: organized, intense, and devoted to her people. Add in Ron Swanson, April and Andy, and the eternally optimistic Chris Traeger, and you’ve got a bang-up workplace comedy. Galentine’s Day alone earns it a spot on this list.

Available to stream on Peacock, Netflix, and Prime Video

If you want found family, you’ll find it at the 99th Precinct; they just all happen to be wearing badges. Much like Friends, the holiday episodes (specifically the Halloween heists) are must-watch TV, plus you get another epic bromance with Jake and Charles. It’ll break your heart a little to laugh at Captain Holt’s endless deadpanning knowing Andre Braugher is no longer with us, but binge-watching his brilliant performance is an homage.

Available to stream on Netflix, Prime Video, and Peacock

Let’s be so for real: If you’re the type who rewatches Friends annually, you most likely have logged at least a few laps through Dunder Mifflin. We couldn’t leave it out, though! Jim and Pam’s slow-burn romance is Ross and Rachel without the “we were on a break” baggage.

Available to stream on Peacock, Prime Video, and Hulu

Sure, the teachers at this underfunded Philly public school are coworkers, but they’re more than that too. They’re a found family who shows up for each other (even if sometimes begrudgingly). Season 6 is airing now, and the show hits its 100th episode this season. If you loved Friends and The Office and haven’t watched this yet, it should move straight to the top of your queue.

If you need an injection of pure dopamine, it’s gotta be Ted Lasso. Here, a relentlessly kind and upbeat American football coach takes over an English soccer club and makes fans of us all. It’s wall-to-wall buddy energy with a side of biscuits! Season 4 wrapped earlier this month, so all four seasons are ready for your binge-watching pleasure.

#8157. The Real Reason We Struggle With Screen Time

How should we all tackle phone use and screen time? An ancient Eleusinian mystery may hold the answer.

Does anyone have a truly healthy relationship with their phone?

I don’t see much evidence of it out there. Personally, the phone is undeniably useful but still feels like a foreign object in my hand — a feeling that was brought into stark relief the second my kids were old enough to pick up a screen. To them, a tablet or phone offers an enticing, comforting, and even productive space. Not healthy, exactly, but familiar. For me, it’s alien — and ground zero for a cultural battle against brain rot, attention loss, and reality itself. Phones stress me out.

I ran into a much needed perspective on this dilemma in a long, thoughtful essay by Karl Ove Knausgaard, the brilliant Norwegian writer with an uncanny ability to see the world as it is, in meticulous detail. My struggle, as he helped me to see, comes from those most influential years in my life — the years before the smartphone. “To understand a man, you have to know what was happening in the world when he was twenty, Napoleon is supposed to have said,” writes Knausgaard in Harper’s Magazine. “The quotation is probably apocryphal, but that doesn’t mean it’s not true.”

My Napoleonic prime was in the 2000s — shortly after the advent of Facebook, but right before the iPhone was in everyone’s hands. For Knausgaard, who is 56 years old, the internet barely existed in his twenties. He admits that he has been ignoring the fundamental influences of such technological advances since. “Not once in those forty years have I turned my attention to technology and tried to understand it,” Knausgaard writes, “how it works in itself, how it works in me. It’s as if I had moved to a foreign country and not bothered to learn its language, as if I am content with not understanding what is happening around me and just settling for my own little world. This lately feels like serious neglect.”

This resonates. While I spend considerable time trying to understand and control the impacts of screen time on my kids' developing brains, I hardly pay attention to my own use. What am I doing when I check for emails, Slack messages, and texts with lab rat-like repetition, or scroll Reddit News and The New York Times at every down moment, or get lost in Instagram and YouTube rabbit holes? More importantly, what should I do about it?

Knausgaard found his technological insight by heading out to Athens, Greece to talk to James Bridle, an author and artist with a specialty in nonhuman ways of thinking (and what orangutans can teach us about politics). In a sense, Bridle sees technology as getting in the way of experience. Sounding like a free range parenting proselytizer, he says that “the only thing you can do is experience it and do it yourself. You have to do it, you have to experience it, it has to happen to you. Bodily, physically — because you’re part of the world.”

Bridle takes this deeper, offering the example of an ancient Eleusinian cult in which initiates were led into a dark room, shown a “whirlwind of impressions, without anyone telling them what they were seeing or what it meant” and being left to interpret that on their own. The next year, they were shown the initiation from the outside, “and you could say that only then, when the gaze from within was complemented by the gaze from without, was the initiation completed.”

This metaphor for the digital world made it all click for me. We’re all too often inside looking at the whirlwind of the internet with little control and understanding. There are more of us now trying to step outside of this world — to see the puppet masters at play in order to walk away from it all.

We’re not going back to 2006, that innocent year before the iPhone was introduced. And I don’t think that should be the goal. The technology that has been introduced since my childhood is incredible, powerful, and a big piece of human progress. But it’s no replacement for the real world lessons I get when I put down the phone and experience life, unfiltered.

Landscape experts reveal how to recreate the striking, sculptural cactus display at Mandy Moore’s former Pasadena home – wherever you garden.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When Mandy Moore put her Pasadena house on the market, most people looked at the interiors. But what stopped me was her living room’s floor-to-ceiling windows, which looked directly onto a patch of massive cacti. In effect, it made her garden look like a living piece of wall art. Architectural, barely any maintenance, and just impossibly cool.

Growing cacti outdoors is much more achievable than you might think, and you don’t have to live in Southern California to do it. I consulted a couple of experts on how you can get this look, too.

Many plants can be quite finicky, and you have to care for them like you would a child or pet. You plant them, water them, tend to them, and eventually, if you’re lucky and the weather cooperates, they reward you with flowers. But, only for a few weeks before they go back to looking like a stick in the ground. Cacti are quite different, fortunately.

Swipe to image 8 to see Mandy's statement cacti:

A post shared by Mandy Moore (@mandymooremm)

Marta Pawlik, Co-Founder and Director of luxury property management company Laik, has used statement cacti across over 50 premium properties and knows exactly what they do to a space: "Cacti serve as great focal points because they fill up the space they occupy without any effort. While most plants ask you to wait for blooms, growth, and seasons, cacti have presence from day one."

Noé Lerma, landscape architect at GreenMex, agrees: "It has forms that are really easy to appreciate on their own. You don't need many to make it look nice. It's a species that doesn't need to be accompanied by other plants."

One plant, one corner, and you’re done. Easy, peasy, organic lemon squeezy.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Mandy Moore is likely growing Euphorbia ammak, which is typically suited for USDA Hardiness Zones 9b through 11b. But the variety you pick should be matched to both your garden size and the visual effect you want to go for.

Pawlik has a clear framework for this: "Golden Barrel cacti (available here on Amazon) work well for small gardens because they group together nicely and allow you to create an intentional look. They tolerate temperatures as low as 20°F (-6°F). Prickly Pear cacti add unique texture to mid-sized gardens and depth where flowering shrubs won't work. Cold-hardy varieties, like Opuntia humifusa (eastern prickly pear), tolerate cold winters down to USDA zone 4. You can order prickly pear at Walmart. For larger properties, Blue Columnar cacti, available on Amazon, are the ones that guests typically capture in photos uninvited."

Lerma's list leans more towards the dramatic, telling me, "Organs, barrel cacti, and Pachycereus are often the most ideal choices for creating a strong visual impact in the landscape."

If you prefer Mandy Moore’s look specifically, columnar varieties are your best bet. Cereus peruvianus, available from Walmart, and Blue Myrtle cactus, from Amazon, both have that striking vertical look that photographs so beautifully and looks super architectural when viewed from indoors.

Often, our first instinct with a dramatic plant is to surround it with other dramatic plants, but this is a mistake.

Lerma is direct on this, telling me, "Avoid placing too many large cacti close to each other. This creates a visual competition between them, rather than allowing each species to stand out on its own." His suggested companions for smaller species: "Natal plum, purple ruellia, fountain grass, and desert rose. And some elements for the soil, such as crushed stone."

A bag of YISZM decorative gravel pebbles (available on Amazon) spread around the base of your cacti pulls double duty. It improves drainage while giving that desert landscape look that ties the whole aesthetic together.

Pawlik shares her most successful pairing to illustrate this point: "Last year I used blue fescue grass with a columnar cactus against dark wooden elements, and all of the guests mentioned this space in their reviews, without prompting."

The formula: one statement cactus, one or two soft companions, and a textured ground cover; resist anything else!

Scale blindness is the most common error. Pawlik has seen it happen, saying, "Recently, one owner traveled two hours to purchase a six-foot Saguaro cactus for his yard, but the cactus appeared unfeasible, and instead of judging the owner's decision, everyone assumed it was an issue." You can buy a smaller specimen from The Cactus Outlet Store via Amazon.

Lerma's advice for avoiding it: "Make sure not to use them too close together. Most of the time, the main objective of a cactus is to be a protagonist element. You can use elements like other desert or xeriscape plants and sculptural stones, but keep in mind to embrace the cactus."

This is the question most people have, and the answer is more encouraging than you'd expect. Pawlik operates properties year-round in the North of England, which is not exactly the Sonoran Desert, with statement cacti: "Hardy Opuntias can withstand harsh winters when the drainage is properly installed and maintained. I have comfortably operated properties with statement cacti year-round with zero maintenance required."

Lerma's approach for cooler climates is equally practical. He tells me, "What we always recommend is to first investigate which type of desert garden you like, then search for species that have a similar look but at the same time can be developed appropriately to your space, and finally make a match between those species. But you should always investigate before planting."

When growing cacti, drainage is non-negotiable, no matter the climate. Cacti will survive cold far better than they'll survive waterlogged roots. Get the soil right – gritty, fast-draining, and ideally amended with horticultural grit or a cactus mix – and the rest will take care of itself. Which, let’s be real, is the whole appeal.

Bonsai Jack's Gritty Mix, available on Amazon, is the easiest way to get that drainage right straight out of the bag. It's specifically formulated to dry out fast between waterings, which is exactly what cacti need and what standard potting compost can never give them.

#8154. What 28 Years Later Can Tell Us About Men Today

Danny Boyle’s zombie trilogy is a timely and important meditation about masculinity.

Will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity? The thought occurred to me as I sat in a theater taking in Danny Boyle’s 28 Years Later the other day. This intense, gory, nudity-laden flick was also one of a surprisingly heartwarming journey for a young boy, Spike, who doesn’t buy into his community’s view of the world. Everyone around him is fearful, incurious, and readily accepts convenient and clear falsehoods about their lives. Spike seeks hope, even if it requires him to face the violent, cruel, and potentially fatal real world off his island.

I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh. In context of the cultural landscape for boys and men today, it’s the kind of exploration we could really use.

Two months ago, Scott Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU and media tour de force affectionately known on his podcast as Prof G, took to The View to talk, as he does so often, about masculinity.

“I like the idea of restoring an aspirational vision of masculinity,” he said to a room that seemed, a bit surprisingly, in total agreement. “I don’t think there’s anything wrong with leaning into your femininity or masculinity if it feels natural.”

In his view, this vision of masculinity involves three pillars: provider, procreator, and protector.

In 28 Years Later, Spike becomes the provider, chasing the health care his mom needs that his dad ignores.

When it comes to the provider, “every man at the outset of his career should take economic responsibility for his household. Sometimes that means getting out of the way” of your more successful partner, he says, and other times it means stepping up. For procreation, he says we should channel “that fire of desire… the right ways [to] make you a better man — kinder, stronger, thinking about how you dress … showering, for God’s sake.”

Finally, he says that in an aspirational vision of masculinity, “your default operating system is protection.” This is a more gentle and empathetic pillar than it might sound on its face. “A lot of women don’t feel safe on the subway,” he explains, “or they see men walking down the street, they cross the sidewalk.” This is due to men eschewing their duty as protector. And “it’s not just physical,” he continues. “When you see a group being demonized, your default setting as a man is you move to protection.”

In 28 Years Later, Spike found himself chasing this view of masculinity headlong: providing the health care his mom needed that his dad would not, protecting her from zombies and himself from indoctrination, not exactly chasing procreation (he’s 12) but rejecting his father’s philandering example. The fact that he lives in a post-apocalyptic landscape in many senses brings clarity to his vision. When there are no worldly comforts, moral clarity arises.

Danny Boyle and Prof G have this in common: They’re both speaking to the broadest possible audiences about things that so many men primarily discuss with, well, other men. With 28 Years Later raking in over $100 million at the box office already and The View’s audience being, well, The View’s audience, it’s refreshing to see such discussion spilling out into the public.

Masculinity is making a comeback. It’s time to talk about it.

#8153. My Kids Love My Toxic Boomer Mom. Why Does It Drive Me Nuts?:

I hate myself for fostering this relationship that feels monumentally unearned, but also I hate myself for resenting it so much.

My children have a special smile they reserve for their grandmother, a sort of twin upturning of the lips and cocking of the head. They love her unreservedly. When they were still little and living at home, the thought of a visit from her was like Christmas. They barely slept before she arrived on our doorstep bearing gifts and hugs and questions and, of course, her own special smile just for them. A similar smile lifting similar lips, a buttery glow of love encircling them all like halos. I have always stood just a little bit outside that circle, their smiles taking a decisive U-turn around my anxious frown.

I am the buzzkill in the room everyone tries to avoid.

It’s not like I don’t love my mom, and it’s certainly not as though I don’t love my children or want them all to love each other. On the contrary, I have spent two decades doing my best to enthusiastically encourage their closeness. I invited her to every school play, every soccer game, every music recital. We spent most of our holidays with her. Her walls are filled with framed photos of my children from me. Her cupboards stocked with mugs about the joys of being a grandmother. Now that they’readults, I update her on all of their accomplishments and downplay any of their struggles. I give her ample content for bragging on social media and long phone calls to her friends.

I hate it sometimes, though: The ease of their love for each other. The falseness of it. I hate myself sometimes for fostering this relationship that feels, in so many ways, monumentally unearned but also I hate myself for resenting it so much.

My mother was not this person with me when I was a child. She lied about everything. She did not hug me or tell me I was good or nice or loved. She parented only when we had an audience and otherwise, I was alone. All the time I was alone. I spent my childhood watching after her, catching glimpses of her as she moved past me and away from me like an accidental celebrity sighting. She was not cruel. She did not hit me or neglect my basic needs. Our home was full of nice furniture. Our fridge full of wholesome food. I had a closet full of clothes that fit me.

It was simply that motherhood was not for her. This was what she told me when I was eight years old. Being a mother was not what she expected, it was boring and annoying and thankless and I really did not bring anything to the table to change her mind. I was just a regular kid like all kids with regular grades and a regular haircut and a regular face. It was never enough to bring her on board.

My children, though, are enough for her. Grandmotherhood, it turns out, is very much for her. She loves the pageantry of it. The constant stream of adoration. She benefits greatly from their clemency, the way they smile indulgently at her obvious lies. Her deeply involved stories in which she is the hero of all things and I am a footnote in their lives if I am mentioned at all. Every moment of my own motherhood stripped away with a few careless sentences at the breakfast table, my face red with frustration and tongue-biting as she erases me from every story. As she slots herself into my absence. As she becomes center stage, yet again.

My children have chided me for getting upset about her lies. They tell me they know the truth, they remember their childhood full of me and us and our lives together where she was simply a benevolent guest. So what’s the harm in letting Gran tell a few harmless fibs. They tilt their heads. They look at each other with doting smiles full of affection. Oh Gran, they’ll say. You know how she is. Don’t let it get to you.

It makes me want to stomp my feet and scream like a petulant child. I want to tell them that yes, I know how she is. That my life has been shaped by “how she is.” That it’s not as easy for me to laugh off her lies, her manipulation, her careless erasure of me and my role as it is for them. They have been gifted with Gran-lite. The watered down, palatable version.

The truth is, they have the relationship I wanted for them. They get to know my unknowable mother in a way I never will. Uncomplicated, easy. Transparent. Someone who lies because she’s old, who is a bit selfish because her days are quiet. Someone who thinks the sun rises and sets on them. Something we have in common.

Maybe it’s simply jealousy. Maybe I wish, even at this late stage of the game, that my mother thought the sun rose and set on me too.

Maybe I wish I was in their little golden circle. All of us smiling at each other. No long, painful history always hiding in the shadows. No one to kill our buzz. Just easy love.
