#8131. 10 Times Ted Lasso Totally Nailed This Whole Parenting Thing

Ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing... or 10.

Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand. Sure, I loved the cheeky ads where an American football coach goes to England to manage a football club. But the premise felt too thin to flesh out into a full series, and Jason Sudeikis’ body of work up to that point didn’t inspire confidence that a sitcom based on the character could hold my attention.

Here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood. Not in a neat, Hallmark-movie kind of way, but in the messy, long-distance, guilt-soaked, love-you-so-much-it-hurts way that a lot of us actually live it. Ted’s relationship with his son, Henry — conducted mostly through grainy FaceTime calls across a six-hour time difference — is the quiet beating heart of all three seasons.

While the rest of AFC Richmond is arguing about formations and tabloid covers, Ted is trying to figure out how to be a good dad from 4,000 miles away while working through how his relationship with his own father has formed him.

The man is not perfect. Nobody raising kids is, and running off to London without your family to accept a job you’re wholly unqualified for as an act of emotional avoidance is a narrative necessity, but it’s a flaw many folks have pointed out.

But along the way, he does his best and makes the right plays in the moments that count. And since parenting lessons wrapped inside a feel-good soccer comedy are my personal favorite delivery mechanism, let’s run through 10 times Ted Lasso gave us a genuine master class in this whole dad thing.

It’s Ted’s first night in London. He’s jet-lagged and disoriented, and the very first thing he does is call home to Henry. He fumbles the time zones and sounds a little lost, but he makes sure his kid hears his voice before the day is out.

There’s a version of Ted Lasso in a different corner of the multiverse who gets swept up in the new job, the new city, the chaos of it all, and phones it in on the fatherhood front. This Ted doesn’t. He knows that presence isn’t always physical. Sometimes it’s a crackling FaceTime connection at midnight your time, 6 a.m. their time, just so your kid knows you’re still there.

Henry, during a video call, asks his dad if he’s ever run into The Beatles over there in England and whether he can get a photo with John, Paul, George, and Ringo. Now, Ted knows that both John Lennon and George Harrison have been dead for decades. He also knows his kid is 8 years old and asking with complete, genuine wonder. So Ted just agrees to try. He doesn't have the heart to kill that particular joy right now.

This one is subtle, but it matters. There's a real parenting skill in knowing when the truth can wait five minutes and when it needs to be delivered immediately. Ted isn't being dishonest — he's being developmentally attuned. There's a season for everything, as a certain king once sang from the stage of a Broadway house, and this particular season called for letting a little kid's imagination breathe. Ted will level with Henry about the hard stuff — and he does, plenty of times — but he picks his moments. That's wisdom.

When Michelle and Henry show up in London, Ted drops everything. They swing by the Crown and Anchor for an authentic English pub experience. They build a double-decker bus model at the kitchen table. And Henry settles into his happy place, sleeping between his parents. Even though Ted is in the midst of a brutal season, managing a locker room full of fragile egos while racking up losses, none of that matters for those few days. He is simply Dad.

What makes this moment rich is what we know that Henry doesn't: His parents' marriage is already over. Michelle is about to tell Ted she wants a divorce. And yet Ted keeps the joy intact for his son. He doesn't let his own grief occupy the visit. That is an act of real parenting discipline — the ability to compartmentalize your own pain long enough to give your child a memory that isn't shadowed by yours. Most of us have had to do some version of this. It doesn't feel heroic in the moment. It just feels hard. Ted does it anyway.

Henry asks Ted why, whenever he sees him on TV coaching soccer, he never seems to be doing anything. It's a kid's question, but it's actually a perfect question. Ted's answer is one of the most quietly profound things in the entire series. He tells Henry that once the game starts, he can't really tell his players what to do — he just has to hope that everything he's been trying to teach them made some kind of dent. Then he says: “It's kind of like being a father.”

And then Henry, having absorbed none of this, is clearly already thinking about something else entirely. Ted realizes midsentence that his kid has mentally bounced. He stops talking. He smiles. He gets it. That moment is the whole job description of parenthood distilled into 30 seconds of television. You pour yourself into the role and hope it lands. You accept that you can't control the outcome. And you find a way to laugh about it — or at least smile — when your kid demonstrates, in real time, that they were not listening. Every parent reading this has lived this exact moment.

Henry isn’t the first kid to idolize a less-than-stellar role model, but his admiration for Jamie Tartt is a particular form of torture for Ted. As enigmatic as he is talented, Jamie makes Ted’s life incredibly difficult, even when he’s scoring goals. This puts Ted in a tough spot as Henry enthusiastically belts out the terribly annoying Baby Shark-themed Jamie Tartt song and sports his jersey with pride.

But Ted lets his son revel in the moment of having access to the talented and popular starlet. He doesn’t even hint at the fact that perhaps Tartt isn’t the best guy to look up to. And when Jamie flashes Ted a smirk that makes his beautiful face even more punchable than usual while signing Henry’s jersey, Ted takes a deep breath and lets his son have a moment he’ll never forget.

Ted gets word from Michelle that Henry has been involved in a bullying situation at school — and then discovers it wasn't Henry who was bullied. Henry was the bully. Ted is shaken. And because of schedules and time zones, he has difficulty getting in touch with Henry right away.

If Ted had been around, he would likely have responded emotionally and sucked all the air out of the room. But when father and son finally get a chance to talk, Henry admits he messed up and didn't follow his dad's advice to count to 10 when he gets angry.

With a little bit of forced space, Henry comes back around on his own. Ted doesn't strip his son of dignity while correcting him. And when Henry apologizes to his friend Doug with a rap in front of the class, you can almost hear Ted beaming through the phone. The lesson Ted had been repeating wasn't wasted — it just needed more time to work. Be a goldfish, sure, but also trust that the seeds you plant eventually grow. Even in the hardest soil.

When Michelle and Henry leave London at the end of their visit, Ted walks them to the gate, knowing his marriage is essentially over and that his son doesn't know it. He says goodbye to Henry the way you say goodbye when you're not sure when you'll see each other again — fully present, holding it together, promising to talk soon. He watches Henry walk away with the airport attendant. And then the mask slips, just for a moment, and you see how much it costs him.

Here's what Ted doesn't do: He doesn't make the goodbye about himself. He doesn't get weepy in a way that burdens Henry with having to manage his father's emotions. He saves that for after the kid is out of sight. This is something parents don't talk about enough — the emotional labor of keeping your own grief off your child's plate. It's not suppression. It's protection. There's a version of this that's emotionally avoidant and unhealthy, but Ted's version in this moment is clear-eyed and loving. He feels everything. He just knows whose feelings need managing right now.

After Henry's visit to London ends and the lad heads back to Kansas, Ted does something small and wonderful. He shows Henry, via video call, that he's placed the miniature Premier League Lego trophy Henry gave him into the Nelson Road Stadium Lego set they built together. It's a tiny thing. It's also everything.

Physical objects carry emotional weight for kids in ways that words sometimes can't. That Lego stadium becomes a shared artifact. It’s something Henry can picture when he thinks of his dad. Something that says “you were here, and you matter, and I kept a piece of what we made.”

It's the parenting equivalent of keeping a drawing on the fridge forever. Henry even notices that Nate's Lego figure is at the back of the bench and asks about it, which gives Ted a gentle opening to explain that relationships can change without anyone being erased. Heavy stuff, delivered through the medium of tiny plastic soccer coaches.

During their Lego video call conversation, Ted tells Henry that he doesn't love the idea of being away from him and that the only reason he's staying in England is that he's doing something important. Henry — who is, let's remember, about 10 years old — tells his dad to try to win the whole thing. Ted pushes back, saying winning isn't everything. And Henry says, essentially: “OK, but at least try.”

That's the moment a kid flips the script on you, and you realize they've been absorbing your lessons all along and also developing their own perspective on top of them. Ted doesn't dismiss the advice. He doesn't say “thanks, buddy” in that patronizing way parents sometimes do. He actually sits with it. He lets Henry be right.

Kids need to see their parents receive feedback and adjust — it's how they learn that it's a normal and healthy thing to do. Plus, Henry is objectively correct. You can care about more than winning and still bring your whole effort to the field. That's not a contradiction. That's maturity.

Ted walks away from AFC Richmond. He turns down the job. He gets on the plane. He comes home to Kansas and, within about 60 seconds, is coaching Henry's junior league team, running plays, completely in his element.

But the real parenting lesson isn't just that Ted comes home. It's why he comes home. He doesn't do it because the job went badly or because England rejected him. He does it because he looked at his life clearly and made an honest accounting of what mattered most. He showed his son — showed Henry in the most concrete way possible — that he is the priority. Not in the abstract, inspirational-poster way. In the literal, I-quit-my-dream-job-in-London-to-be-at-your-soccer-games way.

And then in the finale's final image, when Henry misses a shot and gets frustrated, Ted calls him over. Henry says the words Ted has been saying all series — be a goldfish — and they both smile.

The lesson came back home. Same as the dad.

#8130. Flu season is early this year. Here’s how to actually protect your family, according to experts

For real advice, we talked to two physicians who've spent this fall fielding questions from worried parents.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 16, 2026

It’s almost that time of year when a small cornucopia of medicine takes up residence on the kitchen counter and the house becomes a chorus of coughs and sneezes. As a parent, you know the particular dread of seeing the school nurse’s number flashing on your phone, because you know it’s only a matter of hours until the whole family is flat out.

Unfortunately that call may be right around the corner: Flu season is also arriving months earlier than usual this year.

Experts say it’s a good idea to prepare now before the first fever strikes. Most of what actually protects a family is simple, though, and you don’t need a cabinet full of products or a nursing degree to do it well.

For real advice, we talked to two physicians who’ve spent this fall fielding questions from worried parents. Tracy Tyson, MD and Brittany Odom, MD, are both board-certified pediatricians and moms themselves. Here’s what they want you to know about how to protect your family from the flu this season.

Yes, in parts of the country. “We have started seeing influenza earlier this year, and nationwide reports are also showing an earlier flu season,” Dr. Tyson says. The picture is uneven, though. “Nationally, the latest CDC report shows flu activity is still relatively low but increasing, with the highest activity on the West Coast,” Dr. Odom says, and she’s already seeing plenty of cases in her area. Regions surge at slightly different times, she says, reason enough to get ahead of it now. “You don’t need to wait for flu to fill your child’s classroom before getting them protected.”

Get it as soon as it’s available, both doctors say. “I recommend getting it in September or October, ideally by Halloween, for everyone 6 months and older,” Dr. Odom says. November isn’t too late, she adds, but she wouldn’t wait on purpose, since protection takes about 2 weeks to build and some kids ages 6 months through 8 years need 2 doses at least 4 weeks apart.

“It isn’t ever too late, but the earlier, the better,” Dr. Tyson says. The flu and COVID shots can be given at the same visit, with no required spacing. “As a mom, I know how quickly something on the calendar can get pushed back,” Dr. Odom adds. “So if you have the opportunity now, take it.”

Either one works, if your child is eligible, both doctors say. The shot is approved for children 6 months and up. The nasal spray, or flu mist, is an option from age 2, with limits. “Children ages 2 through 4 with asthma or wheezing in the past year shouldn’t receive the nasal spray, and older children with asthma or other medical conditions need an eligibility review,” Dr. Odom says. Dr. Tyson draws the same line for the mist. Past that, it comes down to your kid. “My priority is an appropriate vaccine that your child actually receives,” Dr. Odom says.

The shot lowers the odds of catching the flu and softens its severity when it breaks through. Dr. Tyson likes an old health-department line. “Taking flu from wild to mild is exactly the right way of thinking,” she says, estimating it prevents flu in up to 60% of cases. It targets influenza specifically, not the parade of other bugs your kid hauls home from daycare. “A sick day after vaccination doesn’t mean the vaccine had no value,” Dr. Odom says, since even a vaccinated child who gets the flu is less likely to end up seriously ill.

If one kid goes down, the rest of the house doesn’t necessarily have to fall like dominos. You absolutely can limit the spread, Dr. Tyson says. The moves that help are unglamorous. Wash hands, stop sharing cups and utensils, cough into an elbow, and separate sleeping spaces where you can. Vaccination cuts household spread too.

You don’t need to disinfect every surface. “Don’t put all your energy into wiping down the house while overlooking the air everyone is sharing,” Dr. Odom says. Crack a window, run a HEPA air purifier, or run the HVAC fan while someone is sick. Masks help during close contact, though never on a child under 2.

And it’s not a failure if another family member gets sick.. “Viruses are sneaky, it happens,” Dr. Odom says.

Most healthy, older kids can ride out the flu at home, but call your doctor if:

Keep a few basics on hand, Dr. Odom says: a thermometer, an oral rehydration solution like Pedialyte, saline drops or spray, and an age-appropriate fever medicine with a dosing syringe. An at-home combination test (which generally covers flu A and B, COVID and RSV in one swab) can also help you tell the flu from the other bugs going around. Care itself is mostly rest, small frequent sips of fluid and saline for congestion. For babies, keep offering breast milk or formula. Honey can soothe a cough for kids 1 and older, but never for a baby under 1.

For fever and aches, acetaminophen helps, and ibuprofen is fine from 6 months, though skip it if your child is dehydrated or vomiting a lot, Dr. Odom says. Dose by weight and use the syringe, not a kitchen spoon, she adds, and never give aspirin to a child with flu.

On how high is too high, the number matters less than you’d think. “There isn’t a level of fever that is unsafe per se,” Dr. Tyson says. “It’s more about the length of time and the symptoms with the fever.” Call the doctor for a baby under 3 months at 100.4°F or higher, and for an older child whose fever repeatedly tops 104°F or won’t come down with medicine. The goal, Dr. Odom says, is a child comfortable enough to drink and rest.

The most vulnerable people in a house can’t protect themselves, so the job falls on everyone else. Babies under 6 months are too young for the flu vaccine, which makes vaccinating the adults and older kids at home especially important, Dr. Odom says. Keep sick visitors away, improve airflow, and for newborns, the advice is obvious but still worth stating since the desire is strong: “No kissing the babies!” The flu shot is safe in any trimester of pregnancy and protects the baby after birth too. For anyone pregnant, immunocompromised or caring for a newborn, don’t wait out a symptom or a known exposure. Call your provider promptly about treatment or prevention.

Asked what they most wish parents knew, both doctors have the same advice: reach out sooner. “You don’t have to wait until your child looks terribly sick to call us,” Dr. Odom says. “Flu has treatments, and timing matters. Asking for help early is part of taking good care of your child, not overreacting.”

#8128. 13 'Practical Magic' Baby Names Sure To Charm You

Who else wants to see a future generation full of baby Jets?

Pop culture baby names don’t always age well (we’re looking at you, Daenerys), but you certainly boost your odds when you pluck a name from a beloved cult classic. And if a timely sequel just happens to arrive right before your own production does, well, even better! That’s why we’re here for Practical Magic baby names.

Alice Hoffman’s bestselling 1995 book spawned a movie by the same name, and its long-awaited sequel, Practical Magic 2, hit the big screen just ahead of the spooky season. True fans know that the saga of the love-cursed Owens women actually spans four books — and we’ve combed through them to find the best Practical Magic names for your own wee witchy woman. Of course, like any good coven, there are 13.

Sandra Bullock’s Sally is fiercely protective and somewhat magic-averse… until she isn’t. The name, originally a diminutive for Sarah, means “princess,” so it’s especially fitting for a little girl. Even better, it’s just starting to climb back up the Social Security Administration’s list of popular baby names, meaning you can jump on this name before the spell of uniqueness is broken.

Practical Magic’s other protagonist is the free-spirited Gillian. Beautiful and impulsive, she’s Sally’s more-fun little sister whose main fault is having terrible taste in men. But let’s focus on the positive, shall we? Gillian — or Jillian — means “youthful,” making it another apropos choice for a baby. And just like sister Sally, it hits that classic-but-not-common sweet spot. Call it baby name magic!

One of the two feisty aunts who raise the young Owens sisters, Bridget is the proper name of Jet and is one of the main protagonists in The Rules of Magic, the second book in the series. Also the name of another literary darling (that’d be Bridget Jones, of course), the Irish name conjures up pluckiness and means “power.”

Hear me out: Aunt Bridget’s nickname is a standout choice for a baby girl all on its own! I mean, if Bridget means power, what more powerful image is there than… a jet? And as played by absolute screen legend Dianne Wiest, Aunt Jet is nothing if not powerful — in both love and magic.

Frances, along with the nickname Franny, is another one of those granny-chic names that is so old-fashioned it feels modern again. (Indeed, it reached number 318 on the SSA’s most recent list of baby names — and Stockard Channing’s return to the role might help it keep soaring.) Plus, it’s wise, eccentric Aunt Frances who has one of the book's most enduring lines: “My darling girl, when are you going to realize that being normal is not necessarily a virtue? It rather denotes a lack of courage.”

Practical and dutiful, Sally’s oldest daughter (played by Maisie Williams in the sequel) grows up to be a med student. But as a name, Antonia has a flowy, delicate feel that’s, dare we say, ethereal in nature. Sitting outside of the top 1,000 baby names, it’s a vintage name that’s more than ready for a comeback. We think it’s spellbinding.

And you thought Kylie Jenner made this name famous! In the Practical Magic series, Kylie Owens is Sally’s youngest daughter (except, oddly, in the sequel, where she’s the elder sister), and she shares her Aunt Gillian’s flaming red hair and rebellious streak. While Kylie as a name is on a bit of a downward trajectory, it’s still a very popular choice, coming in at number 204 on the SSA list.

The original witch and matriarch of the Owens family, Maria mysteriously arrives in America in 1680 (just in time for the Salem witch trials!) and was feared because of her magical gifts. She cast the spell that ultimately cursed any man who fell in love with an Owens woman. What a legacy! As a name, Maria has enduring popularity and multiple meanings, including “beloved.”

Faith Owens is Maria’s daughter and a character in Magic Lessons, the first book chronologically in the series but the third written. Separated from her mother, Faith becomes headstrong and practices blood magic. (Can you blame her?) As a name, Faith has long been a popular choice, although it’s not usually associated with witchcraft!

In Magic Lessons, Hannah Owens is the one who finds baby Maria, raises her, and teaches her the “nameless arts.” She even gives her the “Grimoire”: a leather-bound book of spells. Hannah means “grace” or “favor.”

In Practical Magic, Regina is Sally and Gillian’s deceased mother. While her storyline may not be a happy one, the name itself conjures up regal elegance and means “queen” or “lady.” Dare we say, it’s a magical choice.

Aunt Frances and Aunt Jet’s mother, Susanna stars in the prequel book The Rules of Magic. You won’t find Susanna anywhere on the SSA’s list of the top 1000 baby names, so it’s a clever pick for anyone who wants a name that’s classic but not common.

April Owens is Regina’s mother and Sally and Gillian’s grandmother; she appears in The Rules of Magic. April comes from Latin and means “to open.” It hits that popular-but-not-too-popular sweet spot, ranking at 542 on the most recent SSA baby names list.

If there’s one takeaway from this list, it’s that the baby girl names in the Practical Magic universe are less stereotypically witchy or pop culture-trendy than they are enduringly classic and granny-chic. So tell us: Which name has cast a spell on you?

#8125. Charles M. Schulz Museum With Kids: A Family Guide To Santa Rosa, CA

Between the Charles M. Schulz Museum, a play-forward children’s museum, and dessert-first dinners, this Sonoma County town is basically Charlie Brown’s world IRL.

When the chance came to visit Santa Rosa, California, and experience the Charles M. Schulz Museum, the timing couldn’t have been more perfect. Our little one is ~deep~ in a Snoopy phase. We’ve been rotating Peanuts classics with The Snoopy Show on Apple TV+ because they’re such great low-stimulation wind-down shows before bed (parents included). So Peanuts Gang vibes were definitely what we wanted out of a family trip, and Santa Rosa delivered: walkable cozy dining, cute cartoon sightings around every corner, and plenty for a little kid to get into.

Getting there was definitely the most stressful part because our once-dozing darling of the skies had grown into a ball of energy bouncing around the cabin. Thankfully, the flight was only an hour long from our home base of Los Angeles. Once we hit the road the rest of the way in a rental car, our drive from San Francisco to Santa Rosa washed away the stress as we road-tripped over the water on the Golden Gate Bridge and into the lush greenery of Sonoma County. Visit Santa Rosa hosted Scary Mommy at the Art House Hotel and put together a family-friendly itinerary built around the Charles M. Schulz Museum and the Children’s Museum of Sonoma County, with some of the town’s best food mixed in.

First up was the Poppy Bank Epicenter, where we got to shake loose energy from all the travel sitting. There’s a toddler play area, an arcade, bowling, and Sky Zone, where if your kid is too restless to sit for food, you can pack it up and head over to an activity to tire them out. Ask us how we know. We’re in the restaurant training era, and she was just not having it. Still, Victory House at Epicenter was a great spot; we got massive burgers with fries, plus kids' dino nuggets to go. After a workout on the awesome 4-person Omni Motion VR screen games, we headed back to the hotel to put her to bed and reheat our food.

Here's where Art House really shines for families. Once our little one knocked out, we were able to make use of a full kitchen and sit down at a real dining table to eat like actual adults while still keeping an eye on our snoozing kid. Have you ever eaten cold pizza on a hotel bed in the dark because the baby finally fell asleep? Yeah, then you get why this felt like such a luxury.

The next morning, my husband picked up coffee from Land and Water Coffee, a local roaster with flavorful and sense-awakening brews. It gave us the energy we needed to keep up with our kid, who was raring to go. Our breakfast spot was the Americana, a farm-to-table breakfast nook where we filled up on fresh veggie-packed, cheesy omelets and our daughter happily demolished chocolate chip pancakes with chicken sausage and a milk.

Everything was either walkable or just a short drive away, which meant we could really plan around our kid’s schedule instead of the other way around. Our first big outing of the trip was to The Children’s Museum of Sonoma County, just steps from the Schulz Museum (on the deck for the next day). And it just so happened to be her first-ever children’s museum, so we were just as excited for our precocious kid.

Established by a group of mothers in Sonoma, including Lucasfilm luminaries, the children’s museum grew from a traveling trailer of imaginative play and education into a permanent nonprofit space focused on making fun accessible to local families regardless of income. There’s an admission fee, but families who qualify, including WIC and SNAP recipients, can have it waived through the museum’s family access programs.

The level of love and diversity in every experience was so deeply moving. We started my kid in Totopia, a soft-play woodland nook, because we were nervous to let her roam right away. The staff there were great — not just with her, but with us too, gently coaching Mom and Dad to a place where our anxiety could subside. And with so many safe spaces built for creative play, it didn’t take long for all of us to relax.

Next up was the Wild Zone, a purposeful recreational area full of sticks, climbing, and wobbly unstructured natural play where kids can basically FAFO under supervision. So if they lose their balance by maybe climbing something too ambitiously, they learn consequences. Our kiddo needed that lesson! An experimental FAFO space? Genius, truly.

Outside, our daughter fell hard for the bubble and water tables, because what toddler doesn’t yearn for splish-splashing? Take it from us: You’ll want to pack a change of clothes, because we definitely had to change her before going inside. Back indoors, she “flew” a rocket to space, “cooked” in a retro diner, and “doctored” in the Science & Medical Lab. Then it was back to the hotel for naps all around before heading out on foot to our next family adventure.

Our final day in Santa Rosa brought us to the main event: the Snoopy and Family exhibit at the Charles M. Schulz Museum. Since we had a flight to catch later that day, we swung in for sandwiches at Mac’s Deli (they’re legendary for a reason) and coffee from Espressioso's Coffee, a Latin-inspired roaster specializing in ethically sourced beans.

After getting in a little playtime in the cafe's toddler corner, we made our way to the museum. As animation fans, we geeked out seeing the comic strips up close and learning the story behind Snoopy’s litter of siblings, the focus of the current exhibit. We especially appreciated that it spotlights Bill Melendez, the director and animator behind the Peanuts TV specials — including the one about Snoopy’s origin — as such an integral part of making Peanuts a staple in pop culture.

It was so cool to see how those relatable Snoopy family moments came to life, from being printed on local paper strips by Schulz to the screen by Melendez. In particular, the "Snoopy's Reunion” episode really captures the spirit of Schulz’s work, and how Snoopy’s backstory only made fans love him more. I didn’t know much about Melendez before this visit (including that the Latino animator was the voice of Snoopy himself), and learning about his mark on animation history genuinely moved me. He and Schulz created a vision of childhood still beloved today.

Now I get to share that with my daughter, who is fully in her cartoon dog era. She was surrounded by puppies everywhere she looked, and the giant plush displays of Snoopy with Spike, Belle, Olaf, and the rest of the Daisy Hill Puppy Farm litter gave me full-blown cuteness aggression. Thankfully, there’s a gift shop stocked with Peanuts merch from around the world.

The museum also has art rooms where you can sit down and draw the Peanuts gang, which our daughter loved. Special tables let you trace classic strips and put your own spin on them; I made one to commemorate my little one’s first visit. We also hammed it up in the photo-op installations, including (yes!) Lucy’s psychiatry booth. Nearby, there’s an ice rink where you can skate just like the gang, plus The Warm Puppy Cafe, a Snoopy-themed comfort-food spot serving pot pies, pizza, chili, and hot cocoa.

The whole trip had the gentle, unhurried pace of an idyllic visit to Charlie Brown’s world. All that was missing was a jazz score by the show’s iconic theme composer, Vince Guaraldi! It was lovely to dig into the history of Peanuts and its timeless take on childhood, which Santa Rosa holds onto with such a charming specificity. We’re already plotting a return trip to see if the Great Pumpkin shows up in the fall, or to catch some Charlie Brown Christmas magic.

#8124. The 10 hottest kids’ Halloween costumes of 2026, according to Google

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 20, 2026

Every October, parents become amateur anthropologists, scouring the internet for a Halloween costume that will satisfy one small, extremely opinionated client. (Or, more likely, researching a request for a character we’ve never heard of.)

Now, Google has put all that frantic searching into one place. Its new site, Frightgeist, tracks which costumes are top ranked in search, and the kids’ top ten for 2026 is a gloriously incoherent collection. We’ve got a country legend we’re still mourning, a Thriller-era King of Pop, a web-cartoon jester, and, with no explanation offered, a dumpling.

There’s no tidy theme to sum it up, and I’ve stopped trying. Here’s what you need to know about this year’s top costumes, along with advice for putting a look together.

It just makes sense that our dearly departed Saint of Tennessee comes in at No 1. And since Dolly sported so many iconic looks across a long parade of eras, you have the opportunity to seem like you’re presenting your child with options even when there’s a solid chance this was your idea, not theirs. The only must is a blonde wig that defies gravity. A stuffed bra is optional but encouraged–Dolly would have wanted it that way.

Makes sense she’s spiking, since she’s leading this year’s CMA nominations with nine nods and “Choosin’ Texas” made her the only woman to top the Hot 100, Hot Country Songs, and Country Airplay charts at once. That said, I’ll be honest. Unless said trick-or-treater is belting out “Choosin’ Texas,” this costume will be lost on me. But any excuse to pile on some rhinestones is a good one. (See above.)

The lone non-celebrity in the lineup and, I’d wager, the only costume on this list your kid actually chose for themselves. Chalk it up to the squishy dumpling toys, the brightly colored, bamboo-steamer-packaged squishies that have been dominating TikTok and every kid’s pocket this year. On the plus side, the costume is cozy, warm, and fully nap-compatible. No notes.

Between her two World Cup performances last summer and the early-2000s revival in full swing, she was overdue. I recently combed the attic for my old low-rise jeans, the ones with the half-inch zipper, because my teenage daughter asked for them in earnest. The horror.

Pokémon turns 30 this year, which makes it officially old enough to have trained a generation of parents before becoming their kids’ obsession. Give them a backwards red cap, tuck a Pikachu they already own under one arm, and you’ve got the cheapest, most comfortable costume on the list. Additionally, they’ll be recognizable to every other kid on the block which, for better or worse, is more than I can say for the country singers above.

The show hit its 20th anniversary this year, which means the early-aughts kids who wore out the DVDs are now the ones doing the costume shopping. And if you need another reason to love the pick, Miley is Dolly’s goddaughter, which makes number one and number six a true family affair.

Worth noting that the lone superhero to crack this entire top ten is a woman who also drums in a punk rock band. That’s the kind of role model I can get behind. Spider-Man? Old news. And there’s no new movie to credit here, which means the kids are picking her on pure merit.

Specifically the Thriller era, so we’re talking red leather jacket and at least a loose attempt at the choreography. If your kid can pull off the zombie shoulder roll, they’ll absolutely crush this one. Credit the Antoine Fuqua biopic, “Michael,” that hit theaters last spring and put the moonwalk back in heavy rotation.

Admittedly, I had to look this one up. Turns out, she’s a jester trapped in a digital circus having a slow-motion existential crisis, which tells you this is for the tween and up set–not the toddlers. If your kid is asking for it, they’re too old for the cute stuff and whether you knew it or not, you’re officially in a new stage of parenting. The hat is non-negotiable, though.

Baby Yoda by any other name, and still the single most efficient way to make a small child look even smaller and more adorable. The ears make it truly irresistible and though your stroller may not float, it can still be part of the costume.

And there you have it. Ten costumes, roughly four decades, and one dumpling. Whoever your child opts into being this year, may the wig defy gravity and the candy be plentiful.

#8123. Coach Mando's Advice For Dads Coaching Youth Sports

Brendan Wayne, the man who is The Mandalorian, has been coaching youth sports for more than 20 years. Here’s his advice to other coaches and parents on the sidelines.

When you watch the hit Star Wars TV show The Mandalorian — or the new film The Mandalorian and Grogu — and you start to wonder if there’s something about being a bounty hunter with a heart of gold that can help you with youth sports, you’re not nuts. It’s possible that just through osmosis, thanks to the motions of Mando himself, you’re getting some good sense of how to be a better sports parent. Here’s why: The actor who has played the body of The Mandalorian since 2019, Brendan Wayne, has been coaching soccer for 23 years. In addition to starting a new podcast, Hats & Helmets, Wayne is currently the coach of the Lady Lancers soccer team at Grant High School in California.

“I’ve played sports my whole life,” Wayne tells Fatherly. “It’s one of the greatest things a kid can learn to do.”

As the summer starts to give way to the beginning of school, we reached out to Wayne to get his core principles as a longtime coach of youth sports. This man may know how to calm down Baby Yoda, but that’s just acting. As a soccer coach, Wayne is an even bigger expert. Here’s his clear advice for parents of sporty kids, youth coaches, and why athletics can be great for all kinds of kids.

Wayne’s core coaching philosophy isn’t focused on winning; instead, he feels the only thing that makes a team is the notion of togetherness.

Many parents have been there. The game is going a certain way, and you can’t help yourself with your thoughts. You’ve shouted out something; you’ve even has words with a ref or the coach. What should you do? Wayne’s feelings are very, very clear.

Even as a coach, Wayne doesn’t shout at his players while the game is actually happening. The coaching comes before the game happens, not from the sidelines.

Sometimes, a kid can lose interest in their sport. Or maybe they’re feeling like they’re not part of the team. What can coaches and sports parents do? For Wayne, it’s not about quitting right away but about looking at athletics more holistically.

As an actor and performer, Wayne knows a thing or two about how to keep all aspects of his body in shape — fitting into that Mandalorian armor doesn’t just happen by accident. One of his biggest beliefs, which he applies to youth sports, is that a person has to look at the big picture. For Wayne, it’s all about making sure kids are getting different kinds of exercises.

If you do need to say something to a kid who looks frustrated out there in the game, keep in mind that most of these kids aren’t going pro. Some might, but that’s not the point of this moment.

When Wayne sees one of his kids on the field and they need inspiration, he sometimes just tries to lighten the moment.

George Harrison’s $875 gardening jacket is a design lover’s dream. These alternatives capture the same relaxed, utility-inspired style for less.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

George Harrison may be best remembered as a Beatle, but away from the stage and recording studio, he found another creative outlet in the garden. His historic Friar Park estate in Henley-on-Thames became a lifelong labor of love, with its sprawling grounds offering a retreat from the outside world.

For Harrison, gardening was more than a hobby: it was a way of finding peace, getting his hands dirty and nurturing something over time. That passion is now inspiring a new wave of garden-inspired design, thanks to a collaboration between the Friar Park estate and Japanese gardening brand Niwaki, developed with Harrison’s son, Dhani.

The collection brings together gardening tools and accessories, but it’s the jacket that’s catching everyone's eye... and for good reason! It's taken things well beyond the normal realm of gardening clothes, in the best possible way.

The Friar Park and Niwaki Meditation Jacket (as seen above) is just stunning, isn't it? With its Japanese silhouette, chic denim material, oversized hood, relaxed cloak-like shape and thoughtful detailing, it’s the sort of jacket that makes pottering among the plants feel a lot more stylish.

Think practical workwear with a distinctly design-conscious twist – and it’s easy to imagine wearing it well beyond the garden, too.

There’s just one catch: it costs $875, which is a substantial investment for a jacket you might wear to prune roses, turn the compost or nip out to check on your seedlings. Thankfully, you don’t have to spend nearly a thousand dollars to capture some of that same style, as these alternatives offer different takes on the trend, from a traditional Japanese-style jacket to an everyday barn coat and a practical hooded layer.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

A hanten is a traditional Japanese jacket style, and this one offers a more traditional silhouette rather than a direct copy of the long Niwaki design. Consider it a relaxed layer for pottering around the garden or throwing on over everyday clothes.

Practical, easy to layer and rooted in classic workwear, this longline style offers the utilitarian feel of the Harrison-inspired jacket, while the contrast collar and color-blocked details give it a slightly more fashion-led finish.

If the oversized hood and practical pockets are what caught your eye, this hooded cargo jacket is worth considering. It won’t replicate the original’s cloak-like shape, but it brings some of the same functional details into a more casual category.

If you love the George Harrison-inspired Meditation Jacket but can’t quite justify spending $875, Niwaki’s Engei Lightweight Garden Jacket is worth a look. It has the same garden-minded, Japanese-inspired sensibility, though at $320, it’s hardly an impulse buy either.

The beauty of the original Friar Park x Niwaki jacket is that it doesn’t look like conventional gardening gear. It’s practical, yes, but it also has a distinctive shape and enough style to wear well beyond the garden gate.

Of course, you don’t need to spend hundreds of dollars to give your gardening wardrobe a little more personality. Whether you go for a Japanese-inspired hanten, a classic barn jacket or a relaxed denim layer, there are plenty of ways to borrow the look without breaking the bank.

And as the Beatles once sang, money can’t buy you love – but it might just buy you a rather good gardening jacket.

#8119. The Time Change Wrecks My Entire Family Every Single Year

Apparently, moving the clock one hour is enough to bring our whole household to its knees.

Every year, someone cheerfully announces that daylight saving time is ending as if we have all just won an extra hour of sleep. And every year, I wonder who exactly is receiving this free hour, because it is certainly not the parents.

In my house, the time change does not feel like gaining an hour. It feels like someone picked up our entire routine, shook it like an Etch A Sketch, and handed it back with a smile.

Dinner is suddenly happening at the wrong time. Bedtime feels suspicious. Morning arrives before anyone’s brain has agreed to participate. By 5:30 p.m., it’s pitch-black outside and my body is convinced we have missed bedtime by at least three business days.

People tend to talk about the time change as a problem for parents of babies and toddlers. There are entire survival guides devoted to shifting naps by 15-minute increments so a two-year-old does not greet the day at 4:12 a.m.

But once your child gets older, everyone seems to assume the problem disappears. It does not disappear. The child just gets taller and develops stronger opinions about why bedtime is a government conspiracy.

My son is 11 now. He is not a toddler. He can read a clock. He understands, intellectually, that we moved it back one hour. None of that means his body, brain, appetite, attention span, or emotional regulation received the memo.

The clock may say 7:00, but his nervous system is operating in its own private time zone… and frankly, so is mine.

That is the part I think we miss when we talk about older kids and daylight saving time. We treat it like a scheduling inconvenience instead of what it really is for some families: a disruption to the external cues that help our brains know what comes next.

My son may be old enough to understand what happened, but understanding is not the same as adjusting. Older kids still have circadian rhythms. They still rely on environmental cues. ADHD does not pack its bags and leave just because a child can make his own sandwich. Anxiety does not check the calendar and decide middle schoolers are too mature to be affected by sleep disruption.

And, for the record, adults are not magically immune either. I am 42 years old, and the time change absolutely wrecks me. It takes one dark afternoon for my motivation to crawl into a cave. Suddenly, I am tired at 6:00 p.m., wide awake when I should be sleeping, and personally offended by the sun for abandoning us before dinner.

My brain already has a complicated relationship with time. Moving every clock in the house and changing when daylight appears is not the tiny administrative update society pretends it is.

Meanwhile, life does not pause for adjustment. School still starts at the same number on the clock. Homework still needs to happen. Dinner still needs to materialize through the ancient magic of a mother staring into the refrigerator and hoping the ingredients will organize themselves.

Everyone is more tired, less patient, and somehow surprised that the evening is not going smoothly.

This is usually when parents start blaming themselves.

We think the routine is failing because we have become inconsistent. We wonder why our older child is suddenly moodier, more impulsive, harder to wake, or completely done with humanity by late afternoon. We tell ourselves they should be able to handle a one-hour change.

But one hour is not always just one hour. It is darkness arriving before our brains expect it. It is hunger, attention, sleep, and transitions all showing up slightly out of order. It is the fragile after-school window getting even narrower. It is a child holding it together through seven hours of school and arriving home with absolutely nothing left in the emotional gas tank. It is a neurodivergent parent trying to regulate a neurodivergent child while her own nervous system is also filing a formal complaint.

So this year, I am lowering the bar before the clocks even change. For a few days, dinner can be embarrassingly easy. Bedtime may need to start earlier, even if my middle schooler insists he is basically an adult. Mornings may require more alarms, more light, and fewer unnecessary conversations.

If homework feels harder, emotions run hotter, or we are both staring blankly at each other by 7:00 p.m., I am going to remember that our bodies are adjusting instead of deciding we have suddenly lost every coping skill we ever learned.

I am also refusing to romanticize the whole thing.

Yes, fall is beautiful. Yes, the leaves are gorgeous. Yes, cozy evenings sound lovely in theory. But there is nothing cozy about being trapped in a dark house at 5:45 p.m. with a dysregulated child, an untouched homework assignment, and the dawning realization that bedtime is still hours away.

So if your entire household becomes a little feral when the clocks change, you are not imagining it… and you are not failing.

Keep the routines you can. Add more light, more rest, and more grace where you can find them. Feed everyone something requiring the fewest possible dishes. Give the family a little time to recalibrate.

The clock only moved an hour. Unfortunately, no one told our nervous systems it was supposed to be no big deal.

Danielle Kelly is the host of the ADHD parenting podcast Chaos & Caffeine, which reaches thousands of families each month and was recently named one of the Best Kids With ADHD Podcasts of 2026 by PodRanker.

#8118. The Awkward Truth About Gym Class

Pretend you’re a tree. This was my earliest memory of physical education: our teacher, a tall and thin woman whose broad nimbus of dark hair was edged with gray, asking us to make-believe. By, as I understood it, not moving. In gym class. I was in second grade, and I was already confused. Somewhere here in my elementary school’s wood-floored gymnasium, I knew, there were ropes to climb, mats to tumble on, balls to kick and throw and dodge. And yet we were being corralled into this dumbed-down modern dance — the kind of hippie sh*t, I would later understand, that was typical of our Western Massachusetts college town.

Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class. I was not made for gym. I was small — perpetually the second shortest boy in my grade — and slight and uninterested in the big sports that make up the bulk of public-school gym. I did not own a catcher’s mitt; no sane, responsible adult would let this shrimp play football.

At the same time, I was physical. I was a kid, after all. I wanted to run around, try a handstand, lift a dumbbell, shoot a basket, make a goal. And as uncoordinated and unenthusiastic as I was, I was not entirely untalented. I remember running a seven-minute mile in fourth grade. I could touch my toes and put one foot behind my head. My friend Jason and I competed to see who would be the first to knock out 60 sit-ups in a minute. I don’t remember who won.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class.

Those achievements and activities, however, had nothing to do with gym class as I experienced it. In the same way that English class was not designed to make philistines love literature, or biology to inspire dedication to the scientific method, gym class was not about converting us into athletes. Instead, it was a class for the kids who already were athletes, who played baseball and field hockey for fun, who owned weight machines at home, who didn’t need to sit through the gym teacher’s confounding explanation of what it meant to be “offsides.” I didn’t begrudge them their special class. I could spell and do algebra. They could throw an arcing spiral. This was the way of the world, even in a Massachusetts town full of ex-hippies.

And that all would have been just fine — if gym class had stuck with the most mainstream of sports. I could suck at soccer and blow at basketball, because who cared? Instead, gym class branched out, and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Swimming was a particular source of trauma. When I was 8, during a year my family spent living in Brighton, England, I was so tearfully reluctant to get in the pool that the headmaster of the school had to personally throw me in. And as I got older, the trauma morphed: Back in Massachusetts, the locker room after eighth-grade swimming lessons was a horror movie — I, the underdeveloped shrimp, had to undress surrounded by my Sasquatchian contemporaries. I have a memory of once changing entirely inside a locker, but that can’t be real. Those things were barely 10 inches wide. But another memory is definitely real: During one class, I dived into the deep end — and the force of the water as I entered yanked my swimsuit to my ankles. I don’t know how I had the wherewithal to pull them up before surfacing, but I did. I guess I was learning something.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class. Already awkward around girls, not to mention the implied romance of ballroom dance, I had the misfortune to be paired with Turtle Butt. Who was Turtle Butt? I don’t know. She was a girl I’d never spoken to, but one of my good friends had decided to call her Turtle Butt, even though, as far as I could tell, her butt did not resemble a turtle. And I was going to have to dance with her! Oh, the humiliation!

Gym class has always branched out from mainstream sports — and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Nearly 40 years later, I can now acknowledge that the humiliation was solely in my own head. I remember the potential embarrassment with infinitely more clarity than I remember any actual jeers or taunts, because there were none. But such is the world of the adolescent, where fears and anxieties dwarf reality.

And what I feared most of all was being seen. In other classes this didn’t happen. You might know where the Mason-Dixon Line was — or not. You might know how to deploy the quadratic formula — or not. Either way, you were not exposing anything about yourself other than your intellectual ability, or lack thereof.

It was similar in gym class. We all knew that some kids had it and some didn’t, and there was no shame in being terrible. (Asthma reduced my mile time to 20 minutes by eighth grade. But so what?) The difference, however, was that in gym class, unlike in history or math, you were a physical being. Strip away your ability to perform, and there you still stood, surrounded by your classmates, in sneakers and sweats or the jeans and T-shirt you wore to school that morning. You could pretend you’re a tree all you want — you remained visible: your prepubescent stature, your hairless lack of muscle tone, your terrapin posterior. There were no desks to hide behind, no escape from their eyes and their judgment.

No escape — except, perhaps, to grow up a little. In high school, my family moved to Southeastern Virginia, a place you’d think would have a sports and gym-class culture more extreme than that of the academic Yankees. Instead, gym was even more of an afterthought, not even required after sophomore or maybe junior year. Just like in second grade, I was confused. The school was full of jocks — guys who played soccer and football, girls on the field hockey team — and yet gym class was lackadaisical at best. Driver’s ed occupied a couple of months of the curriculum, and on Fridays, we’d ride a school bus to a nearby bowling alley, where nerds like me, who had no hope of throwing a strike, could at least show off by knowing how to score the game correctly.

Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not.

In fact, I considered the bowling alley my place — because I was there all the time, after school. Technically, not in the bowling alley, but just outside, where almost every day I would meet my skateboarder friends to ride the concrete drainage ditch next to its parking lot. In high school, skating had become my life, my all-consuming hobby, my… my… sport? Yes, my sport! After having failed at all of the mainstream sports, I’d finally found this one sweaty, filthy, wonderful way to be an athlete (though I would never have used that word back then). And while I wasn’t pro material, I wasn’t too bad at it, either. I could hold my own among my friends, at competitions in Virginia Beach, on road trips to Richmond and Washington, D.C. And more important, I could do so without fretting about being seen, in some unspeakable way, by the kids around me. Skateboarding required us to accept one another, in all our foibles and weirdnesses. Because if we didn’t, then who would we skate with?

I stuck with skateboarding for most of a decade, before aging out postcollege and taking up distance running and, more recently, rock climbing. As with skateboarding, I’m pretty good at both, if not truly exceptional, and I appreciate the physical experience of each in ways I could not have imagined in high school. At times, I’ve wondered: If gym class had taught us how to run, or how to scale a boulder, would I have discovered and loved those sports decades earlier? Somehow, I doubt it. Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not. What mattered was what happened after school, in every sense of the term. Still, gym class did teach me this one important lesson about public education: If you make like a tree, you can leave.

#8116. Nobody told me I’d be too busy making the memories to enjoy them

I thought I was giving my kids everything. Instead, I was missing the moments I worked so hard to create.

By Jessica Koosed Etting Updated Oct. 21, 2026

A few weeks before my son Oliver turned eight, planning his birthday started taking up residence in my brain.

We weren’t aiming for anything particularly extravagant. We were having extended family over for dinner and cake, and enjoying the same traditions we’d built around birthdays over the years. Breakfast in bed with balloons. Presents. Time with grandparents. His favorite meal for dinner. And at the end of the night, we’d go around the table and each say three things we loved about him.

These little rituals have become the essence of our family’s birthday magic.

In the weeks leading up to the big day, I was thinking about what Oliver wanted, figuring out the food, doing the shopping, wrapping the gifts, finding cute decorations, coordinating with family about wish lists, ordering the cake, making sure his brothers had something to give him, and remembering the special cereal he wanted. I was doing all of that alongside work and school and dinner and everything else our family already had going on.

Then the birthday came, and it all went off as planned, for the most part. Oliver was thrilled. His brothers were excited. Our family was there. At one point, the boys were all playing and laughing together with their grandparents, and I remember wanting to go sit with them.

Instead, my brain took over. If I didn’t start clearing dinner now, we’d get the cake too late, and we still needed to have time for presents.

So I got up. Set up the cake and dessert. Found the candles I’d bought. Rounded everyone up. Took pictures. And then came more dishes and wrapping paper to clean up and wrangling three tired kids into bed.

Later that night, I sat down and looked through the photos on my phone of everyone smiling together. They were exactly the kind of pictures that make you think, This. This is the good stuff.

But, I couldn’t remember a single moment where I had really enjoyed it or even felt present with my son the whole night. And, unfortunately, birthdays weren’t the only time I felt like this.

I always thought I’d be the type of mom who loved creating fun memories for my kids. Until I became a parent, I never realized how much invisible labor it took to create those magical moments of childhood.

Tooth fairy rituals, holiday traditions, family vacations and weekend outings… They all require someone planning things out in advance. And, usually, that someone is Mom.

To be clear, I love creating fun moments for our family. I know it’s not everyone’s cup of tea, but it wasn’t something I personally wanted to give up. But something needed to change.

Because, while I was busy planning and managing the entire experience, I wasn’t participating. Instead of enjoying my time on the beach with the kids, I was already thinking about who needed sunscreen re-application, or the groceries we’d need to grab for the next day, or the email I needed to send back to their coach.

Some of that is unavoidable. But all of it didn’t have to be mine.

I wish I could say I simply decided to be more present, but it took years to build better habits around how our family plans and shares the work, and I still catch myself slipping into cruise-director mode sometimes.

But as the founder of Jam, an all-in-one calendar and organization app to reduce the mental load of modern family life, I’ve also spent a lot of time thinking about how to better manage the invisible labor that piles up. And over the years, I’ve found some tried-and-true ways to alleviate it, especially during those special magical moments.

Over time, I also realized that some of the most special moments with my kids require absolutely no planning at all. A slow Sunday morning when nobody has anywhere to be. A few extra cuddles and arm tickles at bedtime. The last ice cream cone of summer, before “real life” starts again.

But those moments are also so easy to miss when half your brain is already in tomorrow.

Now I’m better at recognizing that constant pull of the mental load, and pressing pause on it, too.

There will always be something that needs to happen next. I’m a working mom with three kids, after all, so it’s unavoidable.  But I am more aware now that I don’t want to spend their childhood constantly preparing for the next part of it. Sometimes Sunday morning is a good time to get a jump on a few things that need to get done… and sometimes, it isn’t.

When I look back at the pictures, I want to see more than the beautiful moments I created for my kids.

I want to remember how it felt to be there with them, too.

Many parents fear that AI is taking over their teens’ ability to think for themselves. But with some open communication, you can raise kids that are aware of AI’s risks and rewards.

#8114. “I’m Glad I’m The Default Parent” & 49 Other Anonymous Mom Confessions

Seasonal depression, is that you creeping in? Because, fair warning, this week’s confessions are heavy. Sure, we usually have some tough stuff sandwiched between crushes and spicy feelings and your garden-variety MIL woes. But something is shifting, and it seems as though maybe it’s shifting right as our clocks are shifting, too.

And maybe there is something to that. After all, women experience seasonal affective disorder (a type of depression that follows a seasonal pattern) at roughly four times the rate men do. Cool, cool, cool... another thing to add to the list. Oh, and need we mention that mercury is also currently in retrograde?!

Then again, moms are feelers. It’s in our nature. And maybe we’re just feeling the weight of the world on our shoulders even more lately since, well, it’s extra weighty right now. So it’s no surprise that a lot of what moms had to say this week had to do with being at max capacity. Some moms want to rewind to their carefree pre-kid years. Lots are considering leaving their partners. Many just want one day where nobody needs anything from them.

Don’t worry; it’s not all worry and dread. One mom is having the best sex of her life in her 50s (get it, sis). A few are celebrating major milestones.

But whatever’s weighing on you at the moment, just know that somebody in this list has confessed some version of it. Here are this week’s confessions, shared anonymously by moms who clearly needed to lighten their load.

Scary Mommy Confessions are a tried-and-true part of what makes our site so fun. If you want to anonymously confess, look for our weekly callouts on Instagram. And to browse past Confessions, take a look here.

My husband is having the best sex of his life with me. I, on the other hand, am not.

I’ve gone from Needoh hunting to estrogen patch hunting 🙈

I wish I could start my life over and make different choices.

I’m worried my husband is ruining his relationship with our son. They hate each other.

Should I take the leap and become a solo mother by choice? I’m scared.

Still living with my ex and it’s starting to feel weird. I want to leave, but I can’t afford it.

Going through a friend breakup and feeling more relieved than sad. Not everyone is forever.

The long drought is over! 2yrs, 11mos, 2wks & 3 days. Been with my partner 17 years 😤

Our dog passed away and it hurts worse than losing prior family members.

My mom died two years ago this week, and I can’t handle this time of year still so I drink wine.

I never get a break as a single mom and I’m so tired.

Going through perimenopause and my sex drive is much higher than my husband’s. I feel ashamed!

My daughter is overweight like I was and I feel like the world is against her too.

I wish my son’s father would just stop trying to pretend to parent; he’s causing our son anxiety.

I miss something I never had with someone I couldn’t have. I loved him. He didn’t love me.

I really have lost hope that there is romantic love for me out there.

Just once I’d like to come home to the smell of food cooking without me having to plan it.

I can’t afford the holidays this year and idk what to do since they all still believe in Santa.

My husband’s drinking is obnoxious. It’s so unattractive and he is so handsome.

Blasting music in the car when I’m alone just to feel myself again. Even if it’s just for a moment.

I want to run away from my whole life and be a teenager again.

#8113. 10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.

Finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough. But if you’ve got a sporty kid, screen time is a great opportunity. Sure, there’s old-school sports movie like The Sandlot or A League of Their Own — complete with inspirational messages and strong moral codes. But why go for fictional sports stories when you can get the real thing?

Sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes. They tell inspirational tales and maybe even give them a real-life role model in the meantime. From a variety of different sports to a selection of different formats, we’ve thought about the watchability and the relevance of each of these selections. There should be something for everyone in this list. And, at the very least, with each, you and your kid will learn something.

This documentary film focuses on several different Paralympic athletes, all of whom have truly amazing stories. Warning for parents: This documentary is not for the faint of heart, as some of the physical challenges are truly harrowing. For example, Bebe Vio — who inspired the name of the documentary — lost all of her limbs to meningitis at the age of 11. She nonetheless went on to become a wheelchair fencer. Deeply inspiring, this doc is great for teens interested in sports and perhaps great for all of us to have a little perspective on the amazing nature of the human spirit.

The 2004 story of the Boston Red Sox is a great one in terms of an underdog story. Even if you’re not a Red Sox fan, this story represents a very specific time in baseball and tells the story of how this iconic team broke a curse that had existed since 1918. If your kid is just starting to get into baseball, this documentary series might seem like ancient history; after all, 2004 was more than 20 years ago. And yet, this particular season for many of us feels very recent and still relevant.

Who doesn’t love trick shots? This 30 for 30 ESPN doc is all about a group of five guys who were former college roommates who created a sports comedy entertainment phenomenon. Focused on trick shots and betting, this doc is 100% for older kids. But if you’ve got a teen who is into sports and loves to joke around, this is a great, quirky documentary focused on male friendship, humor, and creating something nobody has ever done before.

Everybody is obsessed with Travis Kelce, but his brother Jason Kelce might be the more interesting of the siblings, at least as an athlete. The 2023 documentary film chronicles the 2022 Philadelphia Eagles season, with a specific focus on Kelce. The main tension here is whether or not Kelce will retire from the NFL. Weird topic for kids? Well, for tweens and teens interested in unpacking the real-deal toll of being in the NFL, there’s something smartly educational about this. You may be young and obsessed with football now, but life is long.

Not technically a documentary, this is a docudrama based on the true story of Ray McElrathbey, who deals with a ton of family adversity and racism. Set in the early 2000s, McElrathbey’s story is inspiring and very family-oriented. Again, this one might be for older kids, but the script is from Nick Santora of Reacher and Sopranos fame, so there’s a breezy and very focused feeling to this movie.

Here’s another docudrama that is based on a real-life movement in India, centered on teenagers and skateboarding culture. In the film, a young girl named Prerna (Rachel Sanchita Gupta) finds purpose and belonging through skateboarding. The film is a heartwarming coming-of-age movie, but watching it with your kid means you’re also giving them a dose of contemporary history. The production for the film also worked very closely with rural villages in India to make sure it accurately portrayed the culture and struggles of teenagers.

A great one to watch with your aspiring skateboarding kid, or maybe a kid who isn’t sure what their athletic interest might be.

One of the greatest athletes of our time is also the subject of a one-of-a-kind docuseries. Released in 2024, Simone Biles Rising is all about the gymnast’s comeback. The fact that Biles has been so transparent about her mental health has been a groundbreaking part of the conversations about young athletes. As both a role model and someone who is part of living history, Biles is a figure that should inspire conversation with your curious athlete.

This 10-part documentary changed everything back in 2020. However, at this point, The Last Dance — which tells the story of one of the greatest periods of the Chicago Bulls — almost feels vintage. Chances are, for certain parents, you didn’t have a kid old enough to watch this documentary nearly seven years ago. And, if you’re of the generation that lived through the Bulls’ 1990s dynasty, then you owe it to share that history with your kid.

Not everything about Michael Jordan and his teammates is admirable, to be clear. But the thing about some great sports history is that it can be messy.

Focused on the 2024 X Games, The Rise: Gold Medal Girls of the X Games focuses on four teen athletes, Arisa Trew, Shiloh Catori, Reese Nelson, and Jada Ward. Those are all skateboarders, and that’s just the most recent season. More broadly, The Rise covers all sorts of women’s sports, from skating to the WNBA. If you have a young woman looking for some new role models, you can’t miss with the various seasons of The Rise.

You can really start anywhere with this excellent docuseries. But the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained is focused on the 2024 Tour de France. Obviously, the famous bicycle race has existed since 1903, but it’s really only recently that we could actually document this incredible event. Even the least sporty kid in the world can get excited about people using their bodies to propel a bicycle forward. And the most sporty kids will have trouble wrapping their mind around the sheer effort it takes to traverse 2,200 miles over 24 days over some of the hilliest terrain on Earth.

The most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained, released in 2025, is now the last season of this docuseries. The real Tour de France hasn’t gone anywhere, of course. In fact, it’s happening right now. Meaning if you get your kid excited enough, you can watch the 2026 Tour de France as it’s happening. Or watch a little contemporary Tour de France, then go back and watch Unchained on Netflix.

Scale insects look more like bumps than bugs, making them easy to miss. A careful inspection and timely treatment can prevent them from spreading indoors.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Almost every year in my house, when the porch plants come inside in October, scale insects often come in with them. Adults don't move. Each one sits on a stem or the back of a leaf under a hard or waxy cover, and most people mistake them for rough spots on the bark until the leaves start to yellow.

The best time for controlling scale insects is before the pots come inside. Outdoors, cold nights slow scale down, and lady beetles and tiny wasps eat a share of it. Indoors, the pests have nothing to stop them. They just keep breeding through the winter on whatever plant they came in on.

An adult's waxy shell keeps most sprays from reaching it, making scale harder to get rid of than aphids or spider mites. Newly hatched crawlers have no shell yet. They're the stage sprays work best on, and new ones keep hatching, so treatments have to be repeated.

All scale insects feed through a thin, straw-like mouthpart sunk into a stem or leaf. Brown soft scale (Coccus hesperidum) is rounded or slightly domed, and its covering is part of its body. Armored types such as fern scale (Pinnaspis aspidistrae) are smaller and flatter. Pry one up with a fingernail and the cover usually comes away by itself, leaving the insect behind.

Only the young get around. Crawlers are about the size of a speck of dust, usually yellow or orange, and they spend a day or two wandering before they settle down to feed. Indoors, they cross from pot to pot wherever leaves touch and ride along on hands and pruners. There isn't one hatch to wait out – new ones keep turning up all winter.

Look for small bumps on stems, along leaf veins, and on the undersides of leaves. They can be brown, tan, white, or black. Black scale (Saissetia oleae) is dark, while oleander scale (Aspidiotus nerii) has a pale, nearly round cover. Use a magnifying glass to check plants properly; Carson's TriView folding loupe, available on Amazon, magnifies up to 15x.

Soft scale leaves sticky honeydew on the leaves and on the table under the pot. Black sooty mold, a group of fungi that includes Capnodium species, often grows on it. Badly infested plants show yellowing leaves, leaf drop, and stunted growth. Dead scale can stay stuck for months – press a bump with a toothpick; if it leaves a wet smear, it's alive.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Citrus, jade plants, hibiscus, ficus, bay laurel, oleander, and orchids are some of the most common hosts. Plenty of other tropical houseplants get scale as well, from peace lilies and pothos to palms and snake plants.

Plants that spent the summer outside need the closest look, especially ones that sat close together on a deck or patio. Edible plants like citrus and bay laurel need extra care during treatment, since some products aren't labeled for anything you plan to eat.

An infested plant needs its own spot, starting the day you find scale on it. A spare room is ideal. Otherwise, a windowsill on the other side of the house will do. Wash your hands and tools after touching it.

Leave the plant on its own until several weekly checks in a row turn up nothing new. One crusted with scale from top to bottom is often better off in the trash.

If you only find a handful of scales, there's no need to spray. A cotton swab dipped in isopropyl alcohol loosens them as you rub, and cheap Equate 70% isopropyl alcohol from Walmart is fine for it. Stick with isopropyl, but test it on one leaf first and wait a day or two to see if it leaves marks.

Scale that won't budge usually gives way to a fingernail, a toothpick, or an old soft toothbrush. You can wipe tougher leaves with a soft cloth and a weak dish soap solution, which also removes the honeydew. The shells need to come off, not just get wet. Alcohol doesn't reach the eggs a female keeps under her cover.

Heavier infestations call for a spray. Horticultural oil smothers scale, and insecticidal soap kills the young on contact. Bonide's All Seasons horticultural oil, available on Amazon, comes ready to spray, and for soap, there's Garden Safe insecticidal soap. Coat every stem and both sides of the leaves.

Adults under a thick shell often survive a spray; crawlers don't. More eggs hatch after the first round, so one spray won't finish the job. A common schedule is two or three rounds spaced 10 to 16 days apart, though the label has the final word. Test any spray on a few leaves first, and skip soap on jade plants and ferns, which it can damage.

Broad-spectrum insecticides rarely need to come indoors. Hand removal followed by oil or soap is usually enough.

Keep checking all winter, once a week, and include plants that never had scale. Go slowly over new growth, the leaf joints, and the undersides of leaves. A strip of double-sided tape wrapped around a stem catches crawlers on the move. Under the loupe, they're easy to tell from dust.

Sticky traps won't tell you much about scale. The yellow cards target flying pests, whiteflies (Trialeurodes vaporariorum) and fungus gnats (Bradysia species), both of which turn up indoors in winter. These Safer Brand houseplant sticky stakes from Walmart push straight into the potting mix.

Start outside, before nights turn cold. Go over each plant with the loupe, and treat anything with scale while it's still outdoors. Mix Garden Safe neem oil extract concentrate from Home Depot at the label rate in a Chapin trigger sprayer.

Once plants are inside, keep the ones that summered outdoors apart from the rest for a few weeks. Leave enough space that leaves from different pots don't touch. Check any new plant before it joins the others, too.

Plants that went in clean in October should come out clean in spring. Any that needed treatment can go back outside once nights stay warm. Lady beetles and tiny parasitic wasps live out there, and both attack scale.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.
