#8110. Get Into a Back-to-School Mindset With Advice From 12 Youth Soccer Coaches

Start the school year off on the right foot with insights from coaches who understand how the game translates to life off the field.

Late summer is always the hardest on parents. The pool days are numbered. The long evenings are shortening. The school year is coming, and it doesn’t care how ready you are.

The back-to-school transition is never the clean handoff the calendar makes it look like. Every August, we tell ourselves this year will be different. You’ll get ahead of it. Lunch prep sorted by Sunday. Bedtime routine locked in a week early. Screen-time rules clearly communicated and actually enforced. You’ll draw up this plan with the kind of granular, paranoid attention to detail that Guardiola brings to a cup final. But then, it’s all a disaster by Tuesday.

If you’re looking for an actual strategy that holds up, go to the park on a Saturday morning, find the sideline, and start listening to whoever is coaching.

These are people managing every extreme of human emotion — low blood sugar, wounded pride, full-on existential crises — all while trying to stop a five-way argument over who gets the neon green goalie pinnies. If they don’t know something useful, nobody does. So we hit up a dozen youth soccer coaches for their best back-to-school advice.

I tell my girls this on the first day of every season, and I mean it every time. Some days we’re doing your favorite thing. Some days we’re doing the thing you hate. The thing you hate is usually the thing that needs work. That’s not a coincidence. I don’t let them skip the hard drills because they don’t feel like it. I don’t let them drift to the stuff they’re already good at and call it practice. That’s not practice. That’s just playing around.

The subject your kid is dreading going back to — that’s the one. That’s the drill they need to run. Don’t negotiate them out of it. Make the deal: Do the work first, then we talk. It’s the same conversation I have at practice every Tuesday and Thursday, and it works there, too.

I don’t do big speeches. I never have. I’ve seen coaches do the whole thing — the whiteboard, the clipboard, the fire-and-brimstone season opener — and the kids are bored by the second sentence. So I just ask one question: What kind of teammate do you want? And they tell me. Funny. Helpful. Somebody who doesn’t make you feel bad when you mess up. Somebody who actually passes the ball. I write it all down. Then I say, good — now be all of that.

It’s not complicated. It’s just that nobody asks them the question directly and then holds them to the answer. Try it before school starts. Ask your kid what kind of friend they want to have this year. Then have the second half of that conversation.

I’ve been doing this since before most of these parents were driving their kids to practice, and the one thing that has never changed is this: Effort is the one thing every single kid controls completely. Talent, you’re born with, or you’re not. Height, same thing. But running back on defense when you’re tired? Picking yourself up after a bad touch and going again? That’s a choice. I’ve had kids with every physical tool in the world coast through and wonder why they weren’t improving. I’ve had kids who couldn’t trap a ball if their life depended on it go on to be captains because they simply refused to stop working.

Teachers see it the same way I do. The kid who stays after, asks questions, turns things in on time — that kid builds a reputation. And that reputation opens doors that talent alone doesn’t.

Every season, I get at least one kid who shows up on day one with opinions. Wants to play a different position, run a different shape, do things the way her last team did it. And look — I love that. I want players who think about the game. But there’s an order of operations. You don’t get to redesign a system you don’t understand yet. So the rule is: First month, you learn why we do what we do. Why we press from the front. Why we switch the point of attack the way we do.

Once you understand the why, then you’ve earned the right to push back.

A new school year means new teachers with their own ways of doing things. The kid who spends the first few weeks actually paying attention — figuring out how this classroom works before deciding what they think of it — that kid is so far ahead of the one who comes in with their arms already crossed.

I have a rule on this team, and it has been the same rule since my first season: You get three seconds after a mistake. Three seconds to be upset, to be frustrated, to feel whatever you feel. Then your head comes back up, and you get back in position. Because here’s the thing: The play is still happening. The game didn’t stop because you had a bad touch. And if you’re standing there feeling sorry for yourself, you’re now two mistakes deep instead of one.

I tell parents this, too, because it applies to everything. Your kid is going to fail a test this year. They’re going to say something wrong in class and feel embarrassed about it. They’re going to have a bad day. In life situations off the field, you get more than three seconds, but the same lesson applies. Acknowledge the mistake and then head up, back in position. The recovery is the name of the game.

I am obsessive about communication on the field. Obsessive. Not yelling, not blaming — information. Constant, useful, real-time information between players. Where you are, what you see, what they should do next. Most kids go completely silent under pressure, and that is exactly backwards from what you need. When it’s hardest to talk is when talking matters most.

I tell my players: A quiet team is a confused team. And a confused team gives the ball away. It’s the same thing off the field. The kid who speaks up in class, who says hi to the kid sitting alone at lunch, who tells a friend when something’s wrong — that kid ends up in the middle of things. The good things. Make some noise this year. Say something.

I played college soccer, and I will tell you that the thing nobody taught me until it was almost too late was how to rest. We were all conditioned to think that more was always better — more sprints, more film, more time in the gym. And there’s a point where more just breaks you. The best thing I ever did for my game was learn to take recovery seriously. Sleep. Real sleep. Not optional, not a treat — part of the program.

I build rest into my players’ weeks now, and I don’t let them feel guilty about it. The brain works the same way the body does. It consolidates everything it learned while you sleep. So if your kid is heading back to school and you’re letting them stay up until midnight on their phone — that’s not a small thing. That’s undermining everything they did that day. Rest is not laziness. I promise you it’s not.

I’ve been watching kids show up to this field for a long time, and I can tell you — the ones who get there early are different. Not because they’re more talented. Because they’ve had time to settle in. They’ve already touched a ball, already talked to a teammate, already figured out where they are and what they’re doing before anything’s officially started. They’re comfortable. The ones sprinting in right at the whistle are always the ones who take the whole first half to find their rhythm.

So on the first day of school, get there early. Your kid will have the chance to find the right classroom, ask any questions, and breathe a little bit. It’s a small thing that changes the whole morning.

I coach little kids. Eight-year-olds. So I see a lot of feelings on this field, and I’ve been real clear about my policy since day one: All the feelings are allowed. You can cry. You can tell me you need a minute. You can be upset. None of that is a problem. What you cannot do is walk off this field and decide you’re done. That’s the one thing I won’t accept. And I don’t say it mean — I just say it clearly, and I say it early, so it’s already been said when the moment comes.

Back to school is hard for a lot of kids, and I think parents sometimes feel like they’re supposed to pretend it isn’t. The anxiety is real. The overwhelm is real. Your kid can feel all of it and still go. That’s actually the lesson — that you’re allowed to struggle and still show up. Those two things can both be true at the same time.

I think about the game the way I think about conversation. There are moments when you have to speak — when you see the opening, and you have to take it, because if you wait, it’ll be gone. And there are moments when the best thing you can do is find the person in a better position and give it to them. The hardest thing to coach is the judgment between those two moments. A player who always shoots is a ball hog. A player who always passes is invisible. The great ones — the really great ones — know the difference in real time.

That’s an ego conversation as much as it’s a soccer conversation. Knowing when to speak up in class and when to let someone else take the floor. When to lead a group project and when to step back and support. It’s one of the harder things to teach, and one of the more important ones. Start having that conversation now, before the year starts.

I want my players to come to me. That’s the whole thing. I make myself as available as I possibly can because I know from experience that the kids who ask questions are the ones who get better. Not always the most talented kids — just the ones who seek feedback and then actually do something with it. Every season, the gap I notice most isn’t about skill. It’s about which kids advocate for themselves and which ones wait to be noticed.

Teachers work the same way I do. They want to help — they really do — but they’re managing a roomful of kids, and they can’t chase all of them down. The ones who stay after, send the email, ask what they missed and what they can do better — those are the ones who get more of the good stuff. It’s not about being the favorite. It’s about knowing how to ask for help. That skill will serve your kid for the rest of their life.

I coach at the level where it starts to get serious. Parents are thinking about high school rosters, kids are thinking about highlight reels, everybody’s tracking individual stats. And I am here to tell you — from where I stand on this sideline — that the players who make the biggest difference are almost never the ones you’d expect.

I’ve had physically gifted kids who played every game like it was an audition and made everyone around them worse for it. And I’ve had kids who, by every measurable standard, were average, who won us games because they made their teammates better. They covered for people, they communicated, and they did the stuff that doesn’t show up in the box score.

We spend so much time on our kids as individuals — their grades, their performance, their future — that we sometimes forget to teach them how to be good at being part of something. That’s a skill too. Maybe the most important one. The school year is long and almost entirely a team sport. Remind them.

#8108. 17 Easy Holiday Cocktail Recipes That'll Make You Feel Merry & Bright

Whether you’re hosting a holiday party or just want to sip on a special beverage alone by the fire, now is the time when much of the world goes searching for easy holiday cocktail recipes. We all deserve a little treat after the year that was 2025. Well, rest assured, there’s a fun and festive drink out there for every palate (including if mocktails are more your speed). From spiked hot chocolate and eggnog concoctions for sweets lovers to wintry old-fashioneds and martinis, here are some of the best easy holiday cocktails on the internet.

If you’ve never put Bailey’s in your eggnog, now’s the time. Averie Cooks’ recipe for Santa’s magic potion will help you get the ratio just right, and hit it with a little cinnamon and nutmeg for that perfect holiday flavor.

Mimosas are a crowd-pleasing cocktail, so why not just put a holiday spin on them for your winter party? Damn Delicious’ cranberry mimosas blend orange, pineapple, and cranberry juice with sparkling white wine. Just top with a sprig of rosemary and a couple cranberries and serve.

If you’re not a bourbon fan, might I recommend Princess Pinky Girl’s drunken Rudolph, a hot chocolate cocktail spiked with Fireball instead? This recipe is even less work and is sort of the everyman’s version, if you will.

Family Fresh Meals’ starry night punch recipe is nonalcoholic, but obviously you can just swap the sparkling grape juice for the real thing. It will yield a classic Christmas red sangria, which you can top with star-shaped apple cutouts for the perfect finishing touch.

If you want a cocktail that absolutely screams Christmas, then Dude That Cookz’ peppermint cream martini is the drink for you. It’s a delicious mix of peppermint schnapps, white cream liqueur, and vanilla vodka, with the cutest crushed-candy-cane rim.

Why haven’t I thought of apple cider sangria before? Averie Cooks explains everything you’ll need and how to get the perfect balance of flavors. Then just load ‘er up with apples, cinnamon sticks, oranges, pomegranate, and whatever else your holiday heart desires.

Personally, I swore off blue drinks after one particularly rough hangover in college, but Princess Pinky Girl’s Jack Frost cocktail is admittedly very fun-looking. Just blend your ingredients together, rim your glass, and clink it with a friend’s.

One last mimosa idea before you go, courtesy of Budget Bytes: simply swap out orange juice for apple cider, pour it into your champagne flute until the color is just right, and bada bing bada boom. It doesn’t get any easier than that, and you know it’s going to be delish.

Oh, so you’re having a holiday party party — love that. Then you have to try Princess Pinky Girl’s Instagram-worthy candy cane shots, which only take about five minutes to whip up. Adding a little sweetened condensed milk to the gelatin mix gives it a sweet, creamy base that makes the candy cane flavor really come alive.

Biscuits & Burlap’s spiced pear and chai bourbon drink is the perfect reminder that apples are not the only seasonal fruit worth celebrating. It’s a bit more involved (you’ll need to make a fresh pear simple syrup), but the end result looks so worth that little bit of time and effort.

Speaking of pears, you’ve gotta try Dinners Done Quick’s pear gin fizz. When’s the last time you actually ordered a gin fizz out? They’re so good but they’re never really on cocktail menus anymore, and they give me an old-timey celebratory feel every time.

Moscow mules are the perfect drink to serve to guests if you’re not much of a bartender and you’re just out here doing your best as a host. Fresh Apron’s recipe is a matter of a few simple steps (complete with exact measurements); it’s the festive garnishes and copper mugs that really make this beverage shine.

Savory Spice’s recipe will teach you how to make a chai simple syrup (very useful if you’re an at-home coffee enthusiast, by the way) and how to balance it perfectly within a cranberry fizz. It’ll add a seasonal, cozy depth of flavor that’s unexpected yet oddly perfect.

White russian drinkers, you’ll love this easy apple pie cocktail, made with Crown and RumChata, from Dinners Done Quick. You can easily customize it to make it sweeter, heavier on the cinnamon, extra apple-y, however you take your cocktails.

Be honest: How many gallons of apple cider did you just add to your grocery list?

This article was originally published on Dec. 12, 2025

Timeless Eastern Orthodox baby names that celebrate heritage, culture, and tradition across generations

Have you ever wondered how a name can carry the weight of centuries?

When it comes to naming a baby, tradition often speaks louder than trends. For families connected to Eastern Orthodox heritage, names are more than labels. They’re echoes of centuries of culture, history, and community. These names have been passed down through generations, carrying stories of emperors, scholars, saints, and everyday people who shaped Orthodox life.

From the regal Constantine to the graceful Anastasia, this list of Eastern Orthodox baby names celebrates timeless choices that honor tradition while remaining beautiful and relevant today.

Names are more than words. They’re vessels of memory, culture, and continuity. Within Eastern Orthodox tradition, baby names reflect centuries of heritage, often inspired by Byzantine rulers, revered scholars, and beloved figures whose stories shaped communities across Greece, Russia, the Balkans, and beyond. Choosing an Orthodox baby name isn’t just about finding something elegant; it’s about honoring the past while giving your child a timeless identity that will carry meaning for generations.

From Greek Orthodox names that sparkle with classical charm to Slavic Orthodox names rooted in resilience, these choices embody tradition in its purest form. They remind us that while trends may fade, tradition endures, and a name chosen with care becomes a lasting gift.

#8106. ‘Should I let my kid have ChatGPT?’ and all your biggest questions about AI, answered

Many parents fear that AI is taking over their teens’ ability to think for themselves. But with some open communication, you can raise kids that are aware of AI’s risks and rewards.

By Lauren Ramakrishna Updated Oct. 23, 2026

It feels like artificial intelligence is taking over every facet of life. Adults encounter AI daily. It recommends products for us to buy, shares content we’ll like on streaming platforms, filters spam in our email accounts, and even tracks our health through our smart watches.

It’s increasingly becoming a part of our kids’ daily lives, too. They are accessing AI on smartphones, using it in school and some are even developing relationships with AI chatbots. Fearing a repeat of the consequences that came from unfettered teen access to smartphones and social media in the early 2010s, many parents are justifiably concerned about this new technological frontier.

Experts are sounding alarm bells, as well. Former Google trust and safety executive Tom Siegel recently told Reuters that AI poses a greater harm to children than social media did, highlighting risks such as suicide, psychosis, and reduced critical thinking.

While banning your kids from using AI may sound appealing, it’s not feasible. Unlike social media, which is contained in standalone apps, AI is threaded into technology our kids use everyday, from search engines to video games. That’s why it’s important for parents to focus on AI education to prepare their kids to safely interact with the technology in its many forms.

Whether your kids are just starting to use AI or are already AI connoisseurs, we tapped experts to help answer some of parents’ most pressing questions about teens and AI.

According to a Pew Research Center study, more than half of teens say they have used AI to search for information or get help with their schoolwork. They’re using generative AI, which creates content from prompts, to create images, direct them to research on topics for school and even solve math problems.

Teens are also increasingly interacting with chatbots, which are computer programs that are designed to simulate human conversation. You’ve probably heard of or even used some of the most popular chatbots, like ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini and Perplexity. Roughly two-thirds of teens report using chatbots; 3 in 10 do so daily.

While schools are entrusted with educating young minds to become critical thinkers, AI often takes the thinking away from them. According to the Pew Center study, 59% of teens think students regularly use AI to cheat at school. Of the 15% of teens who said they think AI will negatively impact them personally over the next 20 years, one-third cited overreliance and loss of critical thinking or creativity as major concerns.

While many students think AI provides an easy way to finish their work quickly, doing so has consequences. Kids who heavily rely on AI in high school can struggle in college, where professors are developing methods to identify unacceptable AI use, then handing out failing grades on tests and papers.

In an assignment asking students to compare the Industrial Revolution to today’s digital age, Alcorn State University professor Jason Gibson hid a prompt in invisible white text that would force generative AI to drop the word “Madagascar” into the response in a way that made no sense. He knew students had used AI when he saw “Madagascar” in the completed assignment, and 32 of the 35 students failed a portion of the midterm accordingly.

In 2025, Common Sense Media and Stanford Medicine’s Brainstorm Lab for Mental Health released research showing that three in four teens are using AI chatbots for companionship, including emotional and mental health support. But these programs aren’t providing reliable help and consistently fail to recognize and appropriately respond to mental health conditions that affect young people, according to the report.

And it can have tragic consequences. In August 2025, Matthew and Maria Raine sued OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman after their 16-year-old son Adam died by suicide. The parents allege that ChatGPT coached their son on how to die by suicide, even offering to write a draft of a suicide letter. Adam first started using ChatGPT for homework help, but the chatbot soon became his “closest confidant,” according to the lawsuit.

“Because chatbots show relative competence for homework help and general questions, teens and parents unconsciously assume they’re equally reliable for mental health guidance—but they’re not,” says Common Sense Media. “The empathetic tone and professional presentation mask fundamental limitations that make these systems inappropriate for a use case that affects millions of teens.”

Yes, AI can have positive impacts. “For learning, AI can assist in brainstorming, creating, organizing, summarizing, and synthesizing information, and offering resources and solutions for challenging problems,” according to a statement from the American Psychological Association on AI and adolescent well-being. When used as a tool for guided learning rather than a replacement for critical thinking, AI can ask questions to help challenge a user to analytically approach a topic.

There’s no one-size-fits-all solution for AI use in schools. Depending on where you live, your kids may encounter widely differing expectations. Some school districts are attempting to take a hard pause on AI in the classroom. New York City Public Schools announced that for the 2026-27 school year it has enacted a moratorium on student-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) through eighth grade, with limited use in high schools.

But it’s hard to ban something that in many ways just can’t be escaped. According to a Common Sense Media report on teens and AI, 44% of teens who use AI for schoolwork attend schools where AI tools are blocked—many of them simply switch to personal devices to access AI.

And when schools ban access, educators aren’t able to teach their students how to use AI tools responsibly. Ash Brandin, EdS, a teacher in Colorado’s Boulder Valley School District who shares content to help parents and educators navigate screen time, video games, and digital literacy under the Instagram handle @thegamereducator, says their school district prohibits student access to generative AI platforms on school property. “In some ways, that makes it more difficult [for educators] because it’s very difficult for me to talk about something that is taken further and further away from us,” says Brandin, who uses they/them pronouns.

A staggering 70% of teens say they have never had a teacher discuss how to use AI safely with them, and only 27% have discussed what AI is or how it works with a teacher.

AI is like toothpaste that’s been let out of its tube; trying to get it back in is a fruitless endeavor. Just like adults, “kids are seeing AI woven in and imbued in their everyday lives,” Brandin says.

What teens need is AI education so they can learn what it is, the risks it poses, and how they can use it wisely.

If your teen is using AI for potentially harmful activities, like cheating or for companionship, help them find alternatives. “Think about what your child is getting from the chatbot or AI and what you would like them to do instead,” Brandin advises. Then collaborate with your teen to come up with a plan.

Teaching your kids how to use AI requires more exposure, not less. “I love to explain readiness with a pool analogy,” Brandin says, “I didn’t introduce my child to a pool at the age I thought that they could independently swim. I introduced my child to pools and bodies of water as early as possible.” As babies, you hold them close while they dip their toes. Later, they’re just an arm’s length away while using a floating device. Eventually, they’re diving in the deep end alone while you sit poolside in a lounge chair.

“With each step I’m focused on what skills they need to build up so they have the ability to navigate the pool,” Brandin says. AI is no different. Parents should begin explaining what AI is and how it shows up in our lives as early as possible. Common Sense Media has a free Digital Literacy and Well-Being Curriculum that can help guide age-appropriate conversations about AI, social media, and more.

On their Instagram account, Brandin shares a couple of digital literacy lessons parents can do with their teens, tweens and even younger kids to teach critical thinking skills. The first is to bring up a chatbot and ask it to give a random number between 1 and 100. “If you do that with ChatGPT, 7 out of 10 times it will answer 42,” Brandin says. Ask your kids to react to the results with questions like, “We asked for something random, does this seem random?”

In another experiment, you can ask ChatGPT to explain how to do something that your child already knows how to do really well. “Since our kids are going to AI for things they don’t know, we want to ask it something they know really well so we can turn around and say, ‘It looks like this chatbot made a lot of mistakes on this thing that you know really well. So what do you think is happening when we ask it things we don’t know?’”

I can confirm that my 9-year-old gymnastics-loving daughter had a lot of corrections when we asked ChatGPT how to do a back walkover.

Brandin suggests modeling how to properly and safely use AI. When you are searching, speak out loud and explain to your kids how you are verifying the results AI spits out. What sources did AI use? Do I trust those sources or do I need to look further?

Perhaps most importantly, if your kids are using AI, you need to use it, too. The more you tap into the tools your teens are using, the more you will understand them and be able to communicate with your kids about them.

When you feel fear and anxiety about AI creeping in, “interrogate it for yourself,” Brandin advises. “Are you worried about [your teens] using a chatbot because the information it gives them may be unsafe? Or because they won’t listen to you afterward?” Use your fear to locate the skillset you need to teach your teen.

“It’s very easy to get freaked out about the dangers of AI,” Brandin says. Instead, while we wait for systemic support from governments and tech companies, parents can focus on what they can control at home—open communication, exposure and digital education.

I thought I was giving my kids everything. Instead, I was missing the moments I worked so hard to create.

#8104. 8 Proven Steps to Deter Snakes From Your Garden – and October is the Very Best Time to Take Action

Make your yard inhospitable to snakes in fall and you'll reduce numbers next year, too.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’ve got snakes in your garden then I don’t need to tell you that it’s not the snakes themselves that are the biggest problem, but the constant worry that you might be about to encounter one. Only a quarter of native snake species in the USA are venomous and most – like garter snakes and corn snakes – are helpful garden visitors, eating rodents as well as slugs and bugs. But even if you’re happy to tolerate them as part of a healthy garden ecosystem, it’s smart to set some boundaries and deter snakes from yard areas you regularly use.

October is the very best time of the year to make your yard inhospitable to snakes, if you don’t fancy your garden becoming their permanent winter home. As fall temperatures drop to around 60°F, reptiles will start scouting out a frost-free space to brumate (like hibernating, but not as deep), so now is the time to take action. By making these areas scarce in your garden, snakes will likely move out of your yard to find somewhere to stay. Snakes are also exceptionally hungry in October as they need to store body fat to survive months of winter brumation, so removing food sources will also drive them out of your garden.

And if you need any more motivation to keep snakes out of your garden this month, know that they frequently breed in the exact same space they brumate. A typical female produces 10-30 babies, so if you don’t want a heap more slithering around your garden next summer, here’s your 8-step plan that explains how to deter snakes this fall.

Snakes like cool, damp, dark and undisturbed areas so take a look around your garden to identify probable hiding spots. If you’ve got a large yard and like to share your yard with wildlife, then by all means leave shelter in unused corners. However, in areas of the garden you frequent, clear yard clutter, trim vegetation and bag up fallen leaves. If you have a firewood stack or compost pile, consider moving them further away from the house.

When you’re clearing an area that may already be providing cover for snakes, always use tools rather than your hands. Don’t think that even leather gauntlet gardening gloves will protect you, either, as the single layer of fabric is easily pierced by a snake fang. Gloves are a smart move, but you’ll need animal-handling gloves such as these from Amazon for any worthwhile protection.

Snakes hate spending time in open spaces where they’re visible from the sky and could become easy prey. Especially in October when snakes are highly mobile, keep all grass mown to a length of 3 inches or less and you’ll strongly deter snakes from slithering across it. Be sure to trim transitional zones too, where a mower can’t reach, as these can become favored travelling routes for snakes. A pair of shears with a 90° blade action such as these lightweight Hand Grass Shears from Walmart make short work of trimming lawn edges, or use cordless clippers like this Rechargeable Grass and Hedge Trimmer, also from Walmart.

Dense shrubs provide welcome cover for snakes but it’s an easy task to trim off lower branches to expose the ground and make them less inviting. You can also prune a shrub into the shape of a small tree. Use a pair of pruners – and do sharpen them first with a tool such as a Sharpal, available from Amazon, as cuts made with sharp blades heal much quicker – to cut unwanted branches flush with the main trunk. For bigger branches, a pruning saw like Fiskar’s Power Tooth Pruning Saw, available from The Home Depot, is a better bet.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

We often mulch our garden beds in fall but a cosy, damp layer of pine straw or chunky bark chips offers snakes the ideal spot to regulate their body temperature. Use fine compost to mulch beds and borders instead, which snakes will find far less appealing. If you make your own compost then a rotary sifter such as the Mikiotto Soil Sifter, available from Lowe’s, makes short work of sieving the larger chunks out. Otherwise use a pre-made manure-free compost such as Back to the Roots Organic Compost, stocked at Walmart, as a mulch.

Bird feeders are a prime reason why snakes hang around in gardens. While they don’t eat the dropped seed itself, the reptiles are drawn to the plentiful supply of mice, voles and insects it attracts. And how many of us resume feeding garden birds in fall, just as snakes reach peak appetite?

Getting rid of this easy food source is a key part of the plan to keep snakes out of a garden. The solution is to switch to a waste-free bird food such as Kaytee No Mess Wild Bird Seed, available from Amazon. Hook a seed catcher like this hanging tray from Walmart to the base of hanging bird feeders too, to catch any discarded seed husks.

Fix any gaps that give snake access to a shed, summerhouse or your home. If you need a temporary closure then steel wool is the best way to create a sturdy, weatherproof but non-permanent barrier and bulk packs are available cheaply, such as this steel wool from Amazon. In October, snakes are highly mobile and need the heat of the sun to be mobile, so you’re far more likely to block them out of a hole than seal them in. Do your repairs in the middle of the day when the sun is at its warmest and you can be confident a snake is out basking, hunting or scouting for winter digs.

There are plenty of urban myths that promise mothballs, crushed eggshells and even marigolds deter snakes, but extensive research has proven otherwise. What a study by the USDA National Wildlife Research Centre does show to be an effective snake deterrent is essential oils that are rich in eugenol, namely cinnamon and clove. The research found that this compound irritates the snake’s scent receptor in its mouth and triggers its escape response. So if you're wondering how to keep snakes out of gaps that can't or shouldn't be blocked, here's your solution.

Add 15-20 drops of pure clove oil and the same of pure cinnamon oil to a quart of water in a spray bottle. Add a teaspoon of dish soap to help the oil bind with the water and shake well to mix. Spray this blend around ground vents, woodpiles and decking or porch voids, or anywhere else that gives access to a dark space that can’t be blocked.

Outdoors, oil disperses quickly so reapply after heavy rain or every 2-3 weeks. Once temperatures fall consistently below 50°F, it’s safe to stop as snakes will be holed up in their winter dens.

Snakes are terrified of birds of prey, and one of the easiest ways to deter snakes is to attract owls into your garden. Whether you DIY an owl box or opt for a ready-made design like the Aoibox Large Owl House from Lowe's, October is a prime time to invite owls into your yard as they're actively looking for nesting sites between September and March.

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

#8101. 250 Turkish Baby Names Inspired by Nature, Strength and Beauty

Discover the beauty, meaning, and cultural stories behind 250 captivating Turkish names.

Have you ever met someone and immediately thought, Of course that’s their name?

Maybe their name sounds soft and peaceful, and that is exactly how they carry themselves. Perhaps it feels bold and powerful, matching their confidence before they have even said a word. It can make you wonder how parents choose the perfect name for a baby they have only just met, and how they somehow know which name will grow to suit them.

Choosing a name often means imagining who that baby might become. Parents may be drawn to a particular meaning, family tradition or simply the way a name sounds, hoping it will feel right both in the first moments of life and many years later.

Names become part of how we understand people. Over time, they collect memories, personality traits, family stories and emotions. A name chosen for a newborn may begin with a meaning, a tradition or simply a beautiful sound, but it eventually becomes inseparable from the person carrying it.

Names can carry the same meaning and still sound completely different from one language to another. A name inspired by the moon may feel soft and luminous in one culture, yet bold, mysterious or quietly powerful in another.

Turkish names are especially rich in imagery. Many draw from the sky, the sea, the seasons and the natural world, turning a single word into something vivid and memorable. Aylin evokes a halo around the moon, Deniz and Derya call to mind the sea, Gunes means sun and Yildiz means star.

Others reflect qualities parents may hope their children will carry through life. Eren is associated with wisdom, Mert with bravery and honesty, and Umut with hope.

With roots in Turkic, Arabic, Persian and neighboring traditions, names used in Türkiye reflect a layered cultural history shaped by poetry, nature and generations of meaning.

Below are 100 names commonly used in Türkiye, presented in alphabetical order. The list includes feminine, masculine and gender-neutral options.

Alara – water fairy or mythic river spirit

Ebru – marbled pattern or cloudlike design

#8100. 4 new-school landline phones that help kids chat safely without screens

If your kid wants their first phone, these new options offer 90s nostalgia in spades.

By Audrey Goodson Kingo Updated Oct. 23, 2026

We independently select and share the products we love—and may receive a commission if you choose to buy.

If you fondly recall twirling the phone cord around your fingers while sharing the hottest 4th grade gossip, you can now give your kid the very same experience.

Fueled by Millennial nostalgia for our screen-free childhoods and concerns about online safety, parents are turning to a new-school twist on an old-school concept: the landline phone.

For kids who are craving connection to their classmates but may not be ready for access to the world wide web, these so-called ‘dumb phones’ are a pretty smart alternative.

That’s because smartphones and iPads can be a great way to chat with classmates, but they require a much higher degree of parental oversight. Not to mention, it’s a pain to pry a kid away from an iPad when their FaceTime call is complete.

The new batch of landline phones eliminate those concerns, since they are strictly for talking, and they work via WiFi, with a much lower monthly bill than a traditional landline connection. (And calls between models are free for some of the brands below.)

The 90s are back, baby, and so are the era’s iconic see-through phones, thanks to the latest limited-edition colorway from Tin Can. The company has almost cornered the market on smartphone alternatives, due to its clever concept: The phone’s design is an homage to the days when kids connected tin cans together via string to stay in touch. Nowadays, the phones connect via WiFi, and calls between cans, as they’re called, are free. (So are calls to emergency services.) For $9.99/month, your kid can call any number on an approved contact list. Just like on landlines of old, the cans come with speed dial, voicemail and speakerphone, and you can even set calling hours, so your social butterfly doesn’t chat all night.

The newest entrant on the market, Waffle Home phones are similar to Tin Cans, with a couple more features: The cord is removable, so your kid isn’t tethered to one spot to chat. (A plus or a minus depending on how much supervision you prefer!) Waffle Home phones also have caller ID, giving kids a heads-up before they answer. Similar to voicemail, kids can send voice notes when their friends aren’t free to talk. Like Tin Cans, calls to emergency services and between Waffles are free, but Waffle’s free plan also includes one non-Waffle connection (say, to your cell phone). Unlimited calling to non-Waffle numbers (including international calls to 50+ countries) is $9.99/month.

Ooma is a longstanding, publicly traded telecommunications provider, and its newly-released MyPhone is a great option for parents who want screen-free nostalgia paired with proven reliability. The phone looks exactly like the model every Millennial had growing up, and offers many of the same features as Tin Can and Waffle Home, but at a lower price point. (Calls between Ooma lines are free, and it’s only $7.99/month for a service plan that offers unlimited calls in North America.) Like the Tin Can and Waffle, parents can limit who can call, and kids can receive voicemail messages. There’s even a “party-line” feature for three-way calling when your kid’s gotta dish with more than one friend.

Pinwheel is known for its Android smartphone that offers built-in parental controls, so it’s no surprise the company also launched a landline model for parents who want to give their kids a phone with even fewer bells and whistles. The company’s Pinwheel Home Classic model is another chip-off-the-90s-block, a landline that connects via WiFi and is available at a lower cost than its competition. Calls to 911 and between Pinwheels are free, and the company offers two more calling plans up to $9.99/month for unlimited calls to any external number. As with the other options on our list, parents can manage who can call.

I thought I was giving my kids everything. Instead, I was missing the moments I worked so hard to create.

Let’s face it: Some people are hard to shop for. Whether they say they’re “good with anything” or “don’t need a gift,” they’re mysteries. This list takes the guesswork out of gifting. These things are the ultimate in stuff they didn’t know they needed — and there’s something for every personality. Best of all, they’re impressive without being expensive.

This desktop water pump is a hands-free way to stay hydrated all day. You can add your cup or bottle to its tray, then press the right capacity amount or just have it refill continuously. Small and portable, it's easy to take back and forth between the office and home. It also comes with a USB charging cable and a user manual.

Instead of rummaging in the dark, you can reach for this purse light, which clips onto bags for faster finding. It charges via a USB-C cable and reaches full power in just an hour and a half. After 25 seconds, it turns off, saving power while still giving you enough time to search. With 24 LEDs, it’s extra bright to help you find keys, makeup, and more.

Lead-free and nickel-free, these bracelets are safe for everyday wear. They're also hypoallergenic, so you can buy with confidence, even if you have sensitive skin. They're made of brass and plated with 14-karat gold for an expensive-looking shine. You can mix, match, and stack them, since they come in a set of six.

Hand-painted florals make this soup bowl more of a work of art than a kitchen staple. It has a handle, so you can sip on the go. Made of high-fired ceramic, it’s safe to put in the oven, microwave, and dishwasher. It can handle temperatures up to 480 degrees Fahrenheit. It’s not just for soup, either; it’s a stunning vessel for ice cream, cereal, and anything else you eat from a bowl. You can choose between several gorgeous designs.

You can bring your Pinterest boards to life with these nail art pens, which write smoothly and dry fast. Great for detailing, their ink is waterproof and won't fade, helping your manicure last longer. You can use them at home and in salons, so they're great for nail artists of all skill levels. All you need is a base layer of nail polish to set the scene.

This faux leather bag looks designer without the designer price tag. In its main compartment, it has a pocket to store smaller stuff, like phones and wallets. It’s also wear-resistant, keeping it in like-new condition. With a soft woven texture, it doesn’t have hardware to poke or prod you, except for a convenient buckle closure on the top.

For coffee that stays at an optimal temperature all day, you can try this mug warmer. It sits on desks and other flat surfaces, and it lets you choose between three heat settings. Its LED display and color-coded lights let you know if it's hot or not. You can use it with most ceramic, glass, and stainless steel mugs, putting your whole collection in rotation.

The battery life of these solar lanterns is about eight to 10 hours, so they shine all night. They charge in the sun, glowing without any maintenance when night comes. Their rope hangers give you lots of installation options, from tree branches to wall hooks and everything in between. Reviewers have given them an overall rating of 4.6 stars.

This insulated sleeve keeps cold drinks cold while keeping your hands warm. With double-walled insulation, it's perfect for iced drinks, and its neoprene stretches to fit your cups. Plus, it doubles as a coaster, protecting tables and surfaces. Since you can use it over and over, it’s a smart alternative to paper sleeves.

With eight credit card slots, this RFID-blocking wallet keeps you organized. It creates a barrier against digital theft, keeping private information private. A clear window makes it easier to show your ID when you're out and about. Plus, a zippered pocket protects your small stuff and keeps it all from falling out.

Assorted colors and curved handles give them an artistic touch that brightens up your kitchen. There may be bubbles in your spoons, left over from the firing process, for a magical detail.

With two cords and two ports, this car charger keeps your whole family powered up. It works with standard cigarette lighter sockets, and its retractable cords are 31.5 inches long to reach the backseat. It also has USB-A and USB-C ports for a variety of different models. Plus, its sleek design blends nicely with your car’s interior.

Extra grip helps these claw clips hold your hair up all day. They're made of cellulose acetate, which is plant-based and derived from renewable resources. Their colorful hues and dreamy clouds make accessorizing easier than ever. Plus, they work on all hair types and textures; one reviewer wrote, “They hold my long, thick wavy hair.”

#8096. 300 Beautiful Muslim Baby Names And Their Meanings

150 boy names and 150 girl names, filled with history, beauty, and qualities a child can grow into.

Choosing a baby name can begin with sound, family tradition, or a meaning that catches you at exactly the right moment. Some names feel strong and grounded; others bring to mind light, tenderness, wisdom, or the beauty of the natural world. Then there are the ones that simply sound right when spoken aloud.

Muslim baby names draw from a rich range of languages, histories, and naming traditions. Arabic and Quranic choices appear here alongside other names found within Muslim families and communities. Some are familiar favorites, while others may offer something less commonly heard.

Meanings and English spellings can vary between languages, regions, and transliteration styles, so it is worth checking the pronunciation and cultural context before making a final choice. Ahead, find 300 Muslim baby names and the meanings connected to them.

Ihsan – Excellence; kindness; beautiful conduct

Tahsin – Improvement; enrichment; beautification

Delara – Beloved; one who delights the heart

Layan – Softness; gentleness; comfortable living

Rayhana – Fragrant basil; sweet-scented plant

A beautiful meaning is an important beginning, but a name also lives through pronunciation, family history, and the culture in which a child will grow. Say your favorites with the family name, write them down, and ask relatives how they sound in the languages your child may hear at home.

Often, the right choice is the one that feels natural when spoken and holds something your family hopes to pass on. It may be waiting somewhere in this list, or one name may lead you back to a family favorite you had not considered before. Either way, that moment of recognition is worth waiting for.

Burning bush might be beautiful, but it comes with a whole host of problems. Try instead, then, this native beauty...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I think we're all big enough to admit that burning bush has spectacular autumn foliage, but there’s actually a native shrub deserves a place in the fall color spotlight... one that doesn't come with all the same problems.

As I'm sure many readers know already, burning bush is considered invasive in many states, as it can escape cultivation and spread into natural areas, where it fights with other plants (and usually comes out on top). So, yes, it's well worth looking at native shrubs that deliver that same bold fall foliage without the headache.

And is it too much to ask for more than just that? After all, I'm always drawn to plants that can do more than one job in the garden, so a native shrub that looks beautiful in fall, produces flowers for pollinators, and fruits that can feed birds? Why, it's an absolute must in my books!

So, which native shrub am I waxing lyrical about? Why, it's black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa), a native of eastern North America that is almost criminally underrated by gardeners all over the country... making something like the Viking Black Chokeberry from Nature Hills a brilliant investment for your space!

With its crimson-red to burgundy fall color, black chokeberry typically reaches around 3 to 6 feet tall and wide, making it a useful option for home gardens where a large shrub or small tree might be impractical. It can be planted in a mixed border, used in a native shrub planting, or incorporated into a wildlife-friendly landscape.

Better still? Unlike the pesky burning bush, which is primarily grown for its foliage and compact shape, black chokeberry (as mentioned already!) offers flowers and fruit, making it a standout beauty all season long.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

This native shrub is a happily adaptable one, growing in full sun to partial shade and tolerating a range of soil conditions. It's also generally hardy across USDA zones 3 to 8, although I'd still be sure to check the requirements of a particular cultivar and confirm that it's suitable for your local climate.

In terms of maintenance, it generally doesn't need much intervention once established in a suitable location; just stick to the Three Ds rule when pruning as needed to keep its shape manageable. And otherwise? Well, just sit back and enjoy as its red and burgundy leaves bring the seasonal drama, its white flowers get minibeasts (including your birth month bug) buzzing, and its black berries attract birds like cardinals, waxwings, finches, robins, and more!

Oh sure, burning bush may feel more familiar, but familiarity isn't the only reason to choose a shrub. If I wanted brilliant fall color with the added potential to support local critters, black chokeberry would be at the top of my list... especially if I didn't want to land myself in hot water for planting an invasive beast of a shrub!

#8092. 6 Tips For Getting Through The Holidays When You’re A Mom With ADHD

Strategies for ditching the burnout, surviving the chaos, and rediscovering holiday magic.

Kids losing sleep during the holidays basically a rite of passage. But for moms with ADHD? By that point, the holiday sleep deprivation started weeks ago.

Here’s how mom-of-two Alba C. puts it: “[During the holidays] my mind races to the point that it can take me hours to fall asleep, or fall back asleep. I’ll have thoughts like, ‘Did I buy enough presents?,’ and ‘I have so many presents to wrap!’ Those thoughts start piling up, and that can put me in a moody state where I get irritated very easily.”

Nobody wants to be the holiday Grinch. But when you toss executive dysfunction into the mix with social obligations, family drama, and midnight present-wrapping marathons, the holidays become a brutal obstacle course for moms with ADHD.

“Mothers are often responsible for much of the invisible labor associated with the holidays, from coordinating family schedules, to purchasing and wrapping gifts, moving the Elf on a Shelf, making the ‘holiday magic,’ and keeping a pulse on everyone’s logistical and emotional needs,” explains neuropsychologist Dr. Jessica McCarthy. “For women with ADHD, these responsibilities can become especially overwhelming.”

So moms with ADHD, hear this: You aren’t failing at the holidays — they’re just intense. We talked to experts — and some moms who’ve been through it — to find out how to ditch the burnout, survive the chaos, and rediscover holiday magic this season. Here are some ways to cope.

The holidays amplify struggles with executive dysfunction like forgetfulness, task avoidance, or missing details, explains Dr. Ifeanyi M. Olele, a board-certified psychiatrist with Genesis Psychiatric Solutions. To ease holiday stress, he recommends delegating responsibilities to other family members and asking for help wherever possible.

“Moms shouldn't feel that they have to do everything themselves. If you have a spouse or partner, communicate and divide responsibilities. If there are teenagers or adult children in the house, ask them to help with some of the holiday preparations,” he says.

Holiday parties are where Jacquelyn D.’s ADHD symptoms — including sound sensitivity and social self-consciousness — feel the most intense. To avoid spoiling the party, the 47-year-old mom of two always comes prepared with an escape plan.

“I take a break when I need to, and don't feel bad taking a few minutes to regulate myself,” she explains. “I have some social masking techniques as well, like keeping conversations short and directed outward, and using checking on the kids as a reason to step away and get some fresh air.”

During the merriest season, many moms stay up late wrapping gifts, organizing events, or completing tasks they couldn’t get to during the day. Since sleep deprivation magnifies difficulties women with ADHD are already working hard to manage — like attention, working memory, impulse control, and emotional regulation — Dr. McCarthy advises that sometimes the most productive thing a mom can do is leave something unfinished, and go to bed.

“My advice is to treat sleep as a priority rather than something that happens after everything else is finished,” says McCarthy. “Set realistic cutoff times for holiday tasks, maintain consistent sleep routines when possible, and resist the pressure to sacrifice rest to meet unrealistic expectations.”

One of the biggest mistakes busy moms make during the holiday season is assuming that because there’s technically room on the calendar for another activity, they have the emotional capacity for it, explains Kristen Carder, an ADHD coach and author of You're Not in Trouble: The ADHD Guide to Building Healthy, Connected Relationships.

“If you know that an afternoon with extended family is going to be emotionally taxing, don't schedule another demanding activity immediately afterward. Build in downtime, protect your routines when possible, and pay attention to early signs of dysregulation.”

Amy H., an author and mother of eight, keeps her own ADHD symptoms in check by planning ahead. Her advice? Start your preparations early. Like, early, early.

“Start earlier than feels reasonable,” Amy recommends. “ If the prep is done early, December gets to be about the good stuff instead of the panic. Your future self will thank you — and so will everyone who has to live with that future self.”

While social media scrolls portrays picture-perfect holiday decor and flawless family photos, Emily M., a mom of five, reminds us that real life is rarely as immaculate as it appears through tiny screens — especially for moms with ADHD.

“When I feel myself starting to spiral and feel like I’m not enough, I look at my husband, my kids, and my friends, and I remind myself that I’m worthy even when I’m not perfect. Some days I have to come back to that over and over again, and that’s okay,” she says. “That is the practice.”

Learn more about how to handle your ADHD symptoms at https://www.reframeadhd.com/

#8091. Jefferson Fisher Has The Secret to Getting Along Better With Absolutely Everyone

The lawyer, author, and influencer wants us to talk more and argue less. He might just be onto something.

If being a parent, a husband, a man, a human has taught me anything at all it’s that communication is everything. Also, most of us suck at communication.

For once, our poor communication is not a product of big external forces — neither isolationist politics nor overcooked capitalism nor a failing of modern masculinity. We can only blame ourselves because, hey, communicating is hard. Getting your point across to a group, your nuclear family, or one single person takes practice and discipline, mistakes and learning. I don’t think we ever get it entirely right.

Well, most of us don’t. There are some communicators in this world that are … blessed. Jefferson Fisher is one such individual. Fisher is a Texan, dad, husband, and personal injury attorney who has made a name for himself through social videos that teach us all how to communicate better.

The videos offer pithy lessons like this: Instead of saying I disagree, “tweak it a little and say, I see things differently.” Why? “When you talk in terms of perspective, you find more connection.” Here’s another: “How I talk to my kids will affect how they talk to their kids.”

Simple, pointed, and poignant. You can see why millions tune in.

Fisher’s goal is to make people talk more and argue less. It says just that on the cover of his fantastic, practical, wonderfully written book The Next Conversation — a must read for all of us who strive to get along a little better with those around us.

We caught up with Fisher to talk about his new book and, naturally, anoint him as the latest Cool Dad. Here are some excerpts from our talk, including extras from the Cool Dad Questionnaire and his advice for the most important conversations you’ll ever have.

What’s one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood?

Probably more of a reckless abandon about what they ate. I grew up in just every Little Debbie from Cosmic Brownies to ... everything you could think of that was probably terrible for us, but we didn't know any different.

I mean, this is my guess ... I would say what Sierra loves about me is my steadiness. When things don't go to plan, I'm pretty rock steady. So when there is something unexpected or the kids go into what we call their midnight madness, when it's right there at bedtime and they're absolutely losing their minds, that's when I'm able to step in and I think I'm able to really notice when she's overwhelmed, and take over.

And what do you think they maybe find annoying about you?

I mean, there's lots. I'm trying to find a really good one like she finds the most annoying about me is sometimes I can be a little bit occasionally of like a party-pooper where the kids are just ... all going nuts and I'm like, "Can we just not yell so much in our house?" So there's that.

Probably the bigger thing she gets more annoyed about is my relationship with money. Its just money. So I'm the spender and so she is the saver. If it's something that's like, "Hey, but this would be fun, even though it's not something we exactly need right now, but it would be a cool memory," I think there's a lot of that.

What does fatherhood mean to you in our current world?

Fatherhood, with the caveat of doing it well to be a good father, I think, is knowing it's a discipline and not a destination. It's a daily devotion to putting your wife, your spouse, your partner, your kids before you. And it's this idea of ... are you inconveniencing them for your comfort or is it the opposite, are you willing to inconvenience yourself for their comfort?

There are times where it's going to be uncomfortable. I don't want to be the one carrying all the bags all the time, but is it what my family needs in that moment in the airport? Yeah, that's what they need. Can I do it? Yeah.

I got to say that the carrying bags all the time is a wonderful metaphor.

Yeah. You're the one that is supposed to shoulder the heavy. So you're supposed to carry what they can't. I'm sure there's a similarity to this phrase of to be what others cannot, you must be willing to suffer what others will not, and so it's like that. To be the dad that others can't, you got to be able to do what others won't.

How do you better communicate with your partner in parenting? Do you think there's ways that you, something that don't apply, or do you follow the advice in your book and have great arguments and conversations with your spouse?

I wouldn't say there are things that don't apply. I would say what it would need to go deeper on is the theme of repair specifically. So you could have the mindset of arguments and that's something that's very helpful. There's the idea of saying things with control, meaning be regulated and knowing when you need to take that timeout, and using the pauses. But the turn the book doesn't make with regard to marital relationships is repair.

We are talking about words of affirmation, affirming somebody's feelings, being able to take ownership of your words and what that actually sounds like ... how to truly use words of empathy and affirm how they feel, how to say things that are going to bring. We hit on connection in the book, but more in the way of framing non-relationship conversations.

In repair, there is a lot of something as simple as, "Yes, I said that. Yes, I did that. I absolutely can see how that would have frustrated you or upset you," or "I think it's totally reasonable for you to feel this way. I don't blame you for being upset about that. I could have done that better." And then how to actually, words of apology, how to repair after a rupture, that to me is, that's a whole different ballgame, whole different set of skills.

What do you think about checking in? I'm wondering where that falls in the communication line. It's maybe a little bit of the repair, but is that an important thing to do or how do you feel about just what a felt of unspoken understanding between family?

There's an element that my wife and I do and that's check-ins and check-outs. I mean, it's what we call them, things that we do in the morning and things that we do in the evening. Otherwise, there are times you may never talk to your spouse in the day and you know what that's like. Before you know it, you're just two people, somehow there's a woman who lives with me. I don't know who she is, but she's here and you can be roommates that way if you're not checking in with each other. The other is that unspokenness of knowing when something is wrong and that you feel like you might be approaching things from a different vantage. I like asking the phrase, "What's coming up?" "What's coming up for you?"

Instead of me saying, "What's wrong with you" or even, "What's up with you?" That tends to get a pretty defensive response. But if I say something as simple as what's coming up, there's a difference between [that and] saying, "How are you and how's your heart?"

#8090. Musician Allie Teilz says becoming a mom made her “bigger, not smaller”

The DJ’s debut album, Come to Mommy, is a refusal to pick one version of herself, and a reminder that we don’t have to either.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 23, 2026

It’s dinnertime at Allie Teilz’s house, and the music is already on. Perhaps a film score courtesy of Italian classicist Morricone, maybe some Italian disco easing in behind it. One of the twins, age 3, is already dancing to it. The phones go in the ceramic cow on the counter for the remainder of the evening, where her almost-8-year-old likes them. There’s a projector, a record player, and a wall of VHS tapes with Yellow Submarine and The Land Before Time on heavy rotation. Teilz calls it, half-joking, a ’90s-electronics household.

She is, for the record, impossibly cool. A vinyl DJ and producer who came up in Los Angeles nightlife sharing booths with the likes of Grace Jones and Daft Punk, she now scours thrift stores and estate sales for those VHS tapes and describes herself as “a mother first and an artist second.” She is a mother of four who weaves those two versions of herself authentically into one.

We talked for an hour, and I could have gone three more. Somewhere in the course of our call she made me wish, for a second, that I could do the whole motherhood thing over again. My kids are grown and nearly grown, and I am not in the market for a redo. Still, the childhood she is building for hers, steeped in art and music and curiosity, had me calculating.

Her debut album, Come to Mommy, out now, is the sound of her reclaiming the artist within after the babies arrived. It’s atmospheric, irresistibly dance-able and laced with an electronic vibe that’s both throwback and futuristic. The title turns “come to daddy” on its head. The culture asks what Daddy wants. Teilz would rather ask what Mommy wants, and she answers without flinching. “Mommy wants joy,” she says. “She wants to have fun and dance. She wants pleasure and joy.”

Teilz doesn’t treat her kids as the thing she makes art around. She treats them as the reason her art got deeper. “Becoming their mom,” she says, “only made everything bigger, not smaller.” Motherhood taught her that “the deepest creativity can come from having very little time and knowing exactly what matters.”

There’s a surrender in becoming a parent, she says, a soul handing itself over to lead someone else through life, and for her it cracked the work open instead of closing it down. It “liberated me in creation,” she says, and gave her “a deeper well to pull from.” She has taken to calling motherhood “the highest form of art I’ve ever experienced.”

It changed what she wants to make, too. She looks at her own work through her children’s eyes now and holds it to a single north star. What do I want to see more of in the world? Certainly not  “AI art and lobotomy chic,” her encapsulation of the soulless, machine-driven work she’s watched creep in. She wants her kids to have what she had, the feeling of hearing Talking Heads for the first time and being free, the permission to flail around in  an imaginary version of David Byrne’s giant suit and stay in “that beautiful state of play.” Come to Mommy is her attempt to put that feeling back into the world, and she credits her kids as the inspiration. “They’re the greatest teachers,” she says.

Most women are familiar with the shift that happens when you become a mother. The self gets smaller to make room for everyone else, and for a while Teilz felt it, sliding toward the motherhood she’d watched other women vanish into. The mom groups where everyone gave and gave without ever taking their own needs into consideration. The careers set down and never picked back up. The inability to truly answer the question, “Who am I?” She calls out the insidious culprits that get woven into culture. “We’re indoctrinated by The Giving Tree and The Rainbow Fish,” she says, the children’s books that sell self-erasure as generosity. Make yourself a stump and you’ll be loved. Give away your sparkles and you’ll be accepted. “That’s such a dangerous thing,” Teilz observes.

For a long stretch, her own priorities became submerged. What pulled her back was simple. Boundaries. A flip phone for the hours she refuses to be reachable. She points to a line she saw online, “have boundaries or get an autoimmune disorder,” and says that her health was what finally made her stop. “My kids don’t need a mom who disappears into anything,” she says. “Even motherhood.”

Teilz builds her kids’ childhood the way she builds a record, out of specific, deliberate, slightly magical details. When her daughter earned a leader award at school and got to choose the celebration, she asked to make “ice cream mountains” with scoops stacked into a castle on parchment paper, modeled on the shop Teilz loved as a girl. Ridiculous for the sake of being ridiculous. The memories Teilz recalls most fondly from her own childhood aren’t the cruise or the big trip. They’re the one-bedroom apartment and her mom letting the kids pick a favorite ice cream before the first day of school. Now she makes the small, arguably more impactful kind of memories for her own crew.

There’s also a healthy helping of wonder. The kids get sent out to the garden to pull parsley or a tomato so their hands are involved in making dinner–she’s been teaching them to grow things from seed to fruition for years, because watching a baby artichoke push up from a seed you watered is the kind of small miracle she wants them to appreciate. Books work the same way. She still talks about a woman she once watched on the subway, reading beside her small daughter while the car churned around them, the two of them just reading, an image that stuck with her long before she had kids of her own. Now one of her proudest moments is her daughter climbing onto the couch to get lost in Harry Potter. “Stay curious about the world,” she tells other mothers. “Keep reading. Stay interested in what matters to you.”

None of this came easily. Come to Mommy was written through a brutal stretch that included a traumatic birth, one that nearly cost Teilz and one of her sons their lives, and the album is partly the record of her finding the way back. The final track, Back From the Dead, was written for the twin she almost lost. It’s her way of telling all of her kids that they can come back from the worst thing. Making art out of it was a way to process, and she says, proof to her children that you can take something that breaks you and “make something beautiful out of the ashes.”

Near the end, I painted an image for her. A mom pulls into the driveway and sits in the car a minute before going in, the album still playing. What does she want that woman to carry inside with her? Teilz didn’t hesitate. She wants her to “steal the fire” of her own passion, to think of the song she danced hardest to at her best friend’s 13th birthday, to feel held, to have a reason to dance. Mostly she wants her to feel more like herself.

Not many people tell women that the self doesn’t have to shrink to make room for mothering. Teilz spends a whole album saying it.

I thought I was giving my kids everything. Instead, I was missing the moments I worked so hard to create.

#8088. Don’t Leave These 7 Bulbs and Tubers in the Ground Over Winter – Lift Them Now Before Your Soil Freezes
