From Venus flytraps to corkscrew plants, your birth month carnivorous plant might reveal more about your personality than you think...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On paper, birth month carnivorous plants sounds... well, a little twisted, especially when you compare it to the usual birth month flowers. Most of us have a side to our personality that we don't show the world every day, though, and these plants are the perfect way to shine a light on our dark side.

These remarkable plants are far from ordinary. From the Venus flytrap's sudden snapping jaws to pitcher plants luring in unsuspecting insects, carnivorous plants have developed some ingenious ways to survive. Some are bold and imposing, others are subtle and deceptive, and each and every single one has its own strategy for getting what it needs.

So how does this tie into you? Well, from birth month birds to birth month animals, nature offers us countless ways to reflect on our character. The lens of carnivorous plants, though? Why, that adds a much more intriguing twist! Behind ambition, for example, there may be a need for control. Sensitivity can sometimes turn into possessiveness, while confidence can tip into arrogance. Even our most admirable qualities can have a less flattering side... and there's no point denying it.

Now, we’re already familiar with the idea of a birth month owl, birth month tree, and birth month spider (oh yes, I'm deadly serious!), but carnivorous plants perfectly pair with the traits, instincts and impulses that sit beneath the surface of your everyday personality.

You might be determined to the point of stubborn, much like the Venus flytrap; you might, like the bold pitcher plant, have a more domineering side hidden away. Secrecy, perfectionism or an almost obsessive need to prove a point? Well, sometimes it's worth reflecting on the less flattering habits you might not always recognise in yourself.

Ready to meet your botanical shadow self? Let's dive on in...

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

January babies like to believe they're in control, but their biggest weakness may be their need to have things go their way. No wonder, then, that the Venus flytrap is their birth month carnivorous plant.

Like this iconic houseplant, you know when to strike, and once you've made up your mind, you can be remarkably difficult to sway. You may have little patience for people who waste your time or challenge your authority.

Your dark side emerges when determination becomes stubbornness and protecting your boundaries turns into shutting people out. You don't always give second chances, especially when you feel someone has crossed you. Why not buy yourself a Venus flytrap from Amazon, then, and spend some time watching it and reflecting on what it says about you?

February belongs to the fanged pitcher plant, which feels wholly appropriate. If this is you, then your imagination is one of your greatest strengths, but it can also help you become someone others struggle to read.

Like your birth month carnivorous plant, you know how to draw people in with something fascinating, unusual or irresistible. You may enjoy being unpredictable, keeping parts of yourself hidden and making others work to understand you. And, at your darkest, you can use charm to get your way, leaving people wondering whether they ever really knew you at all.

March babies notice what other people feel, sometimes before they even say it. That sensitivity can make you compassionate, but it can also give you an advantage you don't always use wisely.

Like the sundew plant, you can appear delicate and harmless while holding on tighter than anyone realises. As such, you may struggle to let go of hurt, replaying conversations and remembering every slight. And, when you're wounded, you might use silence, guilt or emotional distance to make others feel the weight of what they've done.

You have a powerful presence and rarely enjoy being told what to do. Indeed, much like the purple pitcher plant, you can draw attention without trying, but your confidence sometimes hides a tendency to rush headfirst into situations you haven't fully considered.

You may mistake resistance for a challenge and disagreement for disrespect. As such, your darker side appears when your need to win becomes more important than understanding others, because you'd rather take a spectacular risk than admit you might be wrong.

Why not treat yourself to a purple pitcher plant from the Ragnaroc Store, then? They're colorful and a cute way to keep pests at bay, not to mention a great way to sit and reflect on the qualities you keep hidden from the world.

If this is your birth month carnivorous plant, you prefer stability... but that doesn't mean you're always as easygoing as you appear.

Like the butterwort, your strategy is subtle: you don't need to chase what you want when you can let it come to you. No wonder, then, that you hide frustration behind politeness, hold grudges long after an argument has ended or quietly keep score when you feel underappreciated.

Your shadow side emerges when patience becomes a way to avoid confrontation and kindness becomes a silent expectation of loyalty in return. Hey, that's not a bad thing; there's a reason this pretty houseplant is so good at killing fungus gnats. Time to bag yourself some butterwort seeds from Amazon, maybe?

A post shared by Lucas Brannen (@lucas_2307_)

Are you a June baby? Say hello to your (very unusual) carnivorous plant!

Always curious about people, you thrive on connection... but you may become restless when the excitement fades. Like the spoon-leaved sundew, then, you attract attention through a delicate and inviting appearance while being far more complicated underneath.

You might tell different people different versions of yourself – not out of malice, but because you want to be understood and liked by everyone. This explains why your darker side appears when the need for validation makes your loyalties unpredictable and your promises easier to break.

A post shared by Singapore Carnivorous Plants (@singaporecarnivorousplants)

Born in the height of summer, July babies care deeply about the people they let into your world, but their loyalty can have a dangerous edge.

If your birth month carnivorous plant is the cobra lily, you present a striking warning to anything that gets too close, and sometimes may convince yourself that you know what's best for the people you love, even when they haven't asked for your help.

No surprises, then, that your shadow side emerges when protection becomes control, jealousy disguises itself as concern and you struggle to accept that the people you love have the right to make mistakes without your permission. Time to pick yourself up some cobra lily seeds from Seedville, then, and pour some love into it.

A post shared by Mobile Bay National Estuary Program (@mobilebaynep)

August belongs to the white-tipped pitcher plant, which means that you (much like your carnivorous friend here) know how to make an impression, and you rarely enjoy being overlooked. Indeed, much like the white-topped pitcher plant, you have a dramatic presence that naturally draws the eye.

Beneath that confidence, though? Well, you may be more dependent on admiration than you care to admit. You might turn everything into a competition, struggle when someone else takes the spotlight, or dismiss criticism as jealousy. Perhaps, then, your darkest tendency is believing (strike that: knowing!) you're exceptional means you should always get your way.

September's birth month carnivorous plant is the rabbit-eared bladderwort, which is incredibly fitting. After all, you notice everything: the inconsistency in someone's story, the mistake everyone else missed, the detail that doesn't quite add up.

Like the water-dwelling bladderwort, your most interesting mechanisms operate largely out of sight. You may appear helpful while mentally cataloguing other people's flaws but, when things don't meet your standards, frustration can turn into criticism, and careful planning can become an obsession with controlling every possible outcome.

Your shadow side, then, is the belief that if you can find a flaw in everything, nothing can ever catch you off guard. An oddly comforting notion, right?

A post shared by Singapore Carnivorous Plants (@singaporecarnivorousplants)

Halloween month (this author's birth month, no less!) belongs to the bowl pitcher plant, a particularly fitting match for anyone who happens to be a little, or a lottle, emotionally evasive.

Oh sure, you know how to keep the peace, but sometimes harmony matters to you more than honesty. Like the bowl pitcher plant, you can thrive in ways that others don't immediately understand; think concealing your real feelings, avoiding difficult conversations or telling yourself that keeping your options open is better than making a decision.

Your darker side emerges when diplomacy becomes avoidance and your desire not to upset anyone leaves others guessing where they truly stand with you.

November babies get a twist on a classic carnivorous plant, in the form of an all-red variety of Venus flytrap. Why? Well, because you rarely feel things halfway. When someone earns your trust, you can be fiercely loyal; when they betray it, you may find forgiveness far more difficult.

Like the Red Dragon Venus flytrap, your dark coloring conceals a mechanism that reacts decisively when triggered. You might dwell on betrayal, replay old arguments or become fixated on proving that someone underestimated you, which means your shadow side appears when you stop seeking closure and start wanting the other person to feel the same hurt you experienced. Eek.

A post shared by 8 Billion Trees (@8billiontrees)

Last but not least, December belongs to the corkscrew plant, which means you are something of an escapist as you crave discovery, freedom and the feeling that something exciting is just around the corner.

Like your birth month carnivorous plant, whose unusual traps lead prey through a one-way route, your own curiosity can take you further than you intended. You may chase new experiences whenever life becomes predictable, abandon plans when they start to feel restrictive or use humor to dodge uncomfortable truths.

Occasionally, your darker side emerges when freedom becomes an excuse to run from responsibility, as every new beginning becomes a way to avoid finishing what you started.

Whichever birth month carnivorous plant you are, and whatever shadowy trait it holds bare to the light, rest assured that you are still a wonderful person (just check out all of your amazingly positive traits in your classic birth month flower).

Still, there's no denying that it can be fun to embrace our dark sides every once in a while... especially if it helps us embrace a whole new world of plants in the meantime. All hail, then, the bitey side of the botanical world! Sometimes, it's good to be bad...

#8021. The Cat Network, Inc. – How a $35 Bounty Started an Epic Journey

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Throughout October, we are throwing our support behind the mission to turn Feral Cat Day into Feral Cat Awareness Month, an opportunity to raise awareness about community cats (also called feral or stray), promote Trap-Neuter-Return, and recognize the millions of caring people who dedicate their time and energy to improving the lives of the cats & kittens most in need of support. With around 60-100 million stray cats in the US, we know it takes more than just one day to make a meaningful difference in a problem this overwhelming, and one group that understands this more than most is The Cat Network in Miami, Florida.

Founded in 1995, The Cat Network is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization supported by more than 2,500 volunteers and donors, helping community cats, stray, abandoned, and homeless cats throughout South Florida while supporting the people who care for them. Through education, low-cost spay/neuter services, adoption assistance, and advocacy, the organization works to humanely reduce cat overpopulation and improve the lives of cats and the communities they live in.

The Cat Network is dedicated to humanely reducing cat overpopulation in South Florida through five core pillars: education, sterilization, adoption, advocacy, and humane public policy. Our story begins more than 30 years agoâ¦

In July 1995, the City Manager of Miami Beach contracted with a commercial trapper, Humane Animal Removal, to trap and euthanize the cityâs feral cats, with a bounty of $35.00 for each cat trapped and killed. When this became public, a local and national outcry ensued, and the media had a field day. The Cat Network, still in its infancy, helped organize local opposition to the trap-kill plan. Susan Fleming, president of The Cat Network and a Miami Beach resident, was instrumental in negotiating with the City to institute TNR instead.  With help from Animal Controlâs mobile animal clinic and SoBe spay/neuter certificates, we convinced the City to implement the more humane approach of TNR.

The following year, we began our spay/neuter certificate program with participating veterinary clinics, the first of which was Galloway Animal Clinic. Since 1995, we've helped sterilize more than 122,000 cats and assisted in the adoption of more than 24,000 cats.

What makes us unique is our comprehensive approach. Rather than simply responding to the symptoms of overpopulation, we focus on preventing future litters while helping cats in need. Our programs include the Miami Meow Mobile, low-cost spay/neuter vouchers, adoption referrals through an extensive foster network, public education, and advocacy for Trap-Neuter-Return (TNR) as the most humane and effective way to manage community cat populations.

One of our biggest challenges is simply the sheer number of cats needing help. Because South Florida has warm weather year-round, kitten season never truly ends. This creates an ongoing demand for spay and neuter services, foster homes, adoptions, and community education. Every day we receive calls from residents who have discovered kittens, injured cats, or growing community cat colonies.

There really isn't an "off season" for cat rescue here, so our volunteers and veterinary programs stay busy throughout the entire year. Preventing unwanted litters through early sterilization is one of the most effective ways to reduce this constant cycle.

Funding is another ongoing challenge. Keeping our veterinary programs affordable requires significant community support, and the costs of medical supplies, equipment, and operations continue to rise.

People can make an enormous difference by:

Becoming a volunteer or foster caregiver.

Sharing our educational resources and adoptable cats on social media.

Every donation, volunteer hour, and shared post helps save lives.

Over the past 30 years, The Cat Network has become one of South Florida's leading organizations dedicated to reducing cat overpopulation. Sterilizing more than 122,000 cats and helping over 24,000 cats find homes are milestones that represent countless lives saved.

We're especially proud of the Miami Meow Mobile, which has dramatically increased access to affordable veterinary care, and our long-standing network of volunteers and foster caregivers who make our adoption program possible. Together, these programs have helped thousands of residents become part of the solution while improving animal welfare throughout South Florida.

The Miami Meow Mobile is a fully equipped veterinary clinic designed specifically for cats. Originally envisioned in 2001 and launched in 2005, it was created to make affordable veterinary care accessible to more people throughout the community.

Today, the Meow Mobile provides low-cost spay and neuter surgeries, vaccinations, testing, microchipping, parasite treatments, and basic wellness services. Originally designed as a traveling clinic, it currently operates from a fixed location in Kendall, allowing us to serve a large number of cats efficiently and safely.

The Meow Mobile remains one of our signature programs because every surgery performed helps prevent future litters and reduces shelter overcrowding throughout South Florida.

Our Spay/Neuter Certificate Program partners with participating veterinarians throughout South Florida. Residents can purchase discounted certificates that cover sterilization surgery, a rabies vaccination, and ear tipping for community cats.

This partnership expands access to affordable veterinary care beyond our own clinic. If someone discovers a stray or community cat in their neighborhood, the voucher program provides an affordable pathway to have that cat sterilized before additional litters are born.

By working together with local veterinary clinics, we're able to reach far more cats than we could alone and give residents practical tools to help solve the community cat problem.

Working with cats means no two days are ever alike. Volunteers have rescued kittens from engine compartments, construction sites, shopping centers, and backyard sheds. Every rescue brings its own surprisesâand often a few scratches and plenty of memorable stories.

The resilience of these cats never stops amazing us. Watching frightened community kittens transform into affectionate family pets is one of the most rewarding experiences we witness over and over again.

Every cat that is sterilized prevents countless future kittens from being born into homelessness. Every adoption changes two livesâthe cat's and the family's.

Knowing that thousands of volunteers, donors, veterinarians, and community members are working together toward the same goal makes every success even more meaningful.

As we celebrate over 30 years of service, our goal remains the same: continuing to expand access to affordable spay and neuter serviceswhile working toward a future where no healthy or treatable cat is euthanized simply because there are too many homeless animals.

We continue to strengthen our community partnerships, grow volunteer involvement, support foster caregivers, and educate the public about responsible pet ownership and Trap-Neuter-Return practices.

Anyone interested in getting involved can learn more by visiting TheCatNetwork.org. There they can become a member, volunteer, foster cats, adopt, donate, or schedule services through the Miami Meow Mobile.

#8020. Dogs on the Screen and in the Audience for Brad Pitt’s New Film

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

You know the drill. Keys in hand. Shoes on. One last look at your dog before you head out, and there they are, wagging their tail like maybe, just maybe, this time you are taking them with you.

Those hopeful eyes. That little head tilt. The expression that says, Excuse me, where exactly do you think youâre going without me?

And then you do the cruelest thing imaginable: you leave.

Sure, they have a perfectly comfortable sofa at home, but imagine settling into a movie theater seat, popcorn in hand, with your dog curled up beside you. Instead of leaving them behind, wondering where you went, you could reach down during the movie and give them a little scratch behind the ears.

Honestly, why have we been doing movie night without them all this time?

Apparently, someone in Miami had the same thought.

At a special screening of Brad Pittâs new movie, Heart of the Beast, at Silverspot Cinema in Downtown Miami on September 19, dogs were officially on the invite list.

The morning had all the ingredients of a proper dog outing: leashes in the lobby, photo ops, plenty of new butts to sniff, and a red carpet where the dogs seemed perfectly comfortable stealing the spotlight.

Then came the part that made this movie night different. The dogs got to go inside and watch the movie, too. And considering that Heart of the Beast is about the bond between a man and his dog, enjoying it in the company of dogs feels almost too perfect.

Heart of the Beast follows Special Forces officer James Belmont, played by Brad Pitt, and his combat dog, Odin, after a plane crash leaves them stranded in the Alaskan wilderness. Their survival depends on communication, trust, and their ability to work together.

The story centers on a relationship that many dog people will recognize, even if the circumstances are a bit more dramatic than the average Tuesday with a Labrador!

Directed by David Ayer and co-starring a German Shepherd named Uber, the movie is described as an adventure thriller centered on the bond between a man and his dog as they face the Alaskan wilderness together.

So while the movie tells the story of one extraordinary human-dog partnership, the Miami screening gave plenty of ordinary dog parents the chance to celebrate their own.

And really, that is part of what makes dogs such irresistible companions. They are not just waiting at home while life happens. They are woven into the little things: the walks, the errands, the road trips, the lazy Sunday mornings; even the occasional movie date.

As fun as dogs in the theater sounds, not every dog is going to be thrilled about it. Crowds, darkness, unfamiliar dogs, and those big cinematic sound effects can be a lot, especially for pups who are sensitive to noise.

Dogs hear much more acutely than we do, so a theater that feels exciting to us can feel pretty intense to them. Around 90 decibels can be uncomfortable for some dogs, and sudden bursts of sound can be especially startling.

A pup who settles happily beside their person? Perfect.

A pup who starts panting, pacing, hiding, or searching for the exit? That is probably their polite way of saying, âI vote for the sofa.â

And honestly, that is okay. Dog-friendly should mean dog-comfortable, not dog-compulsory.

The movie promotion had another very good reason to put dogs in the spotlight.

Ahead of the filmâs September 25 theatrical release, Brad Pitt teamed up with organizations including Wags & Walks Nashville to bring adoptable rescue dogs along to some of the movieâs promotional events.

At a Big Dog Adoption Event in Nashville, Pitt and animal coordinator Andrew Simpson spent time with dogs looking for homes. And at the filmâs global premiere in Franklin, Tennessee, adoptable dogs from Wags & Walks got to join Pitt on the red carpet.

And letâs face it, standing beside Brad Pitt is only going to improve a dogâs chances of finding a new home! Itâs the kind of exposure that can give a little rescue dog a better chance of being noticed. Someone who has never considered adopting might spot one of those faces, click to find out more, and suddenly find themselves filling out the adoption paperwork.

And that is perhaps the most impactful part of all this movie promotion.

The movie gives us a story about the bond between a man and his dog. For these rescue dogs, the hope is much simpler: to find their person, go home, and become someoneâs dog. If Brad Pittâs star power helps a few of these dogs find their forever home, that has to be worth more than any gold statuette.

For the dogs who got to tag along in Miami, they got the kind of movie night most dogs can only dream about: their person right beside them, plenty of new smells to investigate, and a whole theater full of things to sniff. Add a little popcorn to the mix, and honestly, what more could a dog ask for?

#8018. Fall Gardening 101: How to Ripen Green Tomatoes Off the Vine

Many home gardeners associate tomatoes only with summer. And after Labor Day, many move on to fall things, like apple picking and leaf peeping. But the weather is still warm and there are many green tomatoes on the vines. What’s the gardener to do when they have mentally moved on? It seems like such a waste to compost them with the plants. Leaving them on the vine to ripen, though, pushes cleanup into late October, which adds to an already long list of fall chores. Can tomatoes be harvested while still green and then ripened on the counter? Yes, they can! Here are a few pointers to make sure you have the best chance of success.
